title: SPLIT BRAIN: a --wait-for-lease standby acquires the lease while the incumbent is alive
description:
MUTUAL EXCLUSION FAILURE, found by the nidus-lp4.6 work against real minio + valkey. Reproduction is in-tree: tests/e2e/cluster.rs::idle_writer_keeps_its_lease_against_a_waiting_standby, #[ignore]d AND gated behind NIDUS_E2E_XFAIL=1 so it never reddens CI. DO NOT weaken its assertions to make it pass.

SYMPTOM: with a cluster writer holding a healthy lease, a second instance started with --wait-for-lease acquires the lease anyway, within ~2.4s, against an 8s lock_ttl. Both instances then report role=ClusterWriter and holds_writer_handle=true with different owner tokens. Observed via GET /cluster on both:
  writer:  lease_owner 98105-1784992862827886000
  standby: lease_owner 98106-1784992865248226000

ONE CAUSE FOUND AND FIXED in the same change (do not re-introduce): ClusterLease had #[derive(Clone)] added so a renewer could hold a handle, but ClusterLease is an OWNING GUARD whose Drop deletes the lease object. Every cloned handle therefore released the lease when dropped, leaving the lock object briefly ABSENT — which a peer's create-if-absent walks straight through. Confirmed from an instrumented S3 delete: 'delete key="lock" | renewing lease | delete key="lock"' on the WRITER. Fixed by introducing a Drop-free LeaseRenewer (backend/object.rs) and removing Clone from ClusterLease. The writer no longer deletes its own lock.

A SECOND DEFECT REMAINS — this issue. After that fix the standby STILL acquires. What is known:
- try_claim's create-if-absent probe returned Some(false) on the standby's first attempt (so minio DOES honour If-None-Match) and Some(true) on a later attempt ~250ms on, meaning the lock object was absent again at that point. No S3 delete of "lock" is logged from the writer after the fix, so the disappearance is currently unexplained.
- An instrumented staleness check showed confusing state that undermines the above trail: ttl=2 when the instance was started with --lock-ttl 8, and a stamp that never advanced. Either the TTL is not being plumbed to the claim path, or those log lines came from a different instance than assumed. RESOLVE THIS FIRST — it may well be the whole bug (a claim path using a default 2s TTL instead of the configured one would explain a premature takeover exactly).

WHY IT MATTERS: safety of committed DATA is still protected by CAS on every durable write (the stalled-writer fence test passes), so this is not known data loss. But two writers both believing they hold the handle is a mutual-exclusion break, and it makes --wait-for-lease (nidus-lp4.3) unsafe to recommend for production until fixed.

SUGGESTED NEXT STEP: instrument ClusterLease::acquire and try_claim to log the instance's own pid, the configured ttl, and the key, then re-run the repro — the pid will settle whose log lines are whose, which is what defeated this pass.
acceptance_criteria: With a healthy cluster writer holding the lease, a --wait-for-lease standby never acquires it; the repro passes with NIDUS_E2E_XFAIL=1 and is then folded into the normal suite.
close_reason:
FIXED (v0.33.0). The reported symptom was already resolved by the Clone-on-owning-guard fix in PR #58 — the repro passes 3/3 in isolation and in the full parallel suite, with tracing showing the writer renewing every ~2.7s and the standby correctly reading age=0-3s against its 8s TTL. The 'second defect' was diagnosed from pre-fix evidence (and the confusing ttl=2 line was a concurrently-running test: LOCK_TTL_SECS is 2).

Investigating with pid-tagged lease tracing (NIDUS_LEASE_DEBUG=1, kept in-tree) surfaced four REAL protocol defects that could each produce the same two-owners symptom. All four are fixed, each guarded by a test verified to fail without the fix:

1. RENEWAL WAS A READ-MODIFY-WRITE RACE. renew_lease_object did get-then-UNCONDITIONAL-put, so a peer that reclaimed the lease between the holder's read and its write was silently overwritten — the holder stamped its own ownership back and carried on, while the peer also believed it held the lease. Now a put_cas gated on the token from the same read. A lost CAS is re-read before concluding anything, so an instance racing ITS OWN other renewer (op-driven vs the server timer) is not fenced by mistake.

2. STALENESS MATH WAS OFF BY UP TO A SECOND. Stamps are whole seconds, so an age computed from two truncated stamps can overstate real elapsed time by nearly 1s; a strict age<ttl declared a live, renewing holder dead. Now age<=ttl (see is_live). Takeover lands in ttl..=ttl+1s.

3. A TRANSIENT BACKEND ERROR PERMANENTLY FENCED A HEALTHY WRITER. check_writable latched fenced on ANY renew error, so one dropped connection retired the instance for good. Now only the typed LeaseLost signal latches; a blip fails the write in flight and nothing more.

4. A BACKGROUND RENEWAL LOSS WAS ONLY PRINTED. fenced was latched solely by a failing write, so a superseded writer with no traffic kept answering /ready 200 and reporting holds_writer_handle=true indefinitely — exactly the two-owners window. LeaseRenewer now shares the store's fenced latch (Arc<AtomicBool>).

The repro is folded into the normal suite un-gated (assertions unchanged, plus a new explicit holds_writer_handle assertion), joined by a_superseded_writer_discovers_it_is_fenced_without_any_write. Full cluster suite 14/14, whole e2e target 26/26 against real minio+valkey.

title: Fsync::OnFlush still fsyncs the data file on every upsert, so it delivers half the speedup it promises
description:
`Store::upsert` phase 2 (src/store/write.rs) calls `self.data.sync()` UNCONDITIONALLY:

    // Phase 2: fsync data before writing log records.
    if let Err(e) = self.data.sync() { ... }

Phase 4, the log sync immediately below it, is correctly gated on `self.config.fsync == Fsync::PerBatch`. Phase 2 is not. So a store opened with `Fsync::OnFlush` — documented as 'fsync only on explicit flush()/close (faster, weaker durability)' — still pays one full disk barrier per upsert CALL.

MEASURED (nidus-bench-write, release, macOS/APFS where sync_all is F_FULLFSYNC; dim=384, batch=1):
  store append, Fsync::OnFlush    ~3.8 ms per upsert call  (should be ~0)
  additional cost of PerBatch     ~3.7 ms per upsert call
  => OnFlush buys 50%, not the ~100% the flag implies.
Constant across store sizes (50 / 200 / 800 calls all ~3.8ms), confirming it is one fixed barrier per call and not work that scales with rows.

At batch=1000 the same barrier is amortised to ~3.7us/vector, which is why this has been invisible: it only shows up on small batches, which is exactly the shape a per-request HTTP writer produces.

WHY IT LOOKS SAFE TO GATE. The write-order invariant (SPEC §6.2) is that a log record must never be durable while the data row it references is not. Under OnFlush neither file is synced until `flush()`, and `flush()` already syncs in the same order (data, then log — src/store/write.rs:541-542). The crash state the per-call sync would prevent is precisely the one the documented reader rule already handles: replay ignores any record referencing a row >= data_size/dim, so a log-ahead-of-data tail is detectable and recoverable, never torn. That is also the durability contract OnFlush advertises ('a crash can lose acknowledged writes').

NOT FIXED IN THE PR THAT FOUND THIS (nidus-xb9 measurement) on purpose: it is a one-line guard but it changes crash-recovery behaviour on the durability path, and it deserves its own review and its own crash/recovery test rather than riding along in a benchmarking change.

ACCEPTANCE
  * Gate phase 2 on `Fsync::PerBatch`, matching phase 4.
  * A test that OnFlush + kill-before-flush recovers to a consistent (possibly shorter) store — the log-ahead-of-data tail must replay cleanly.
  * Re-run `just bench-write`: OnFlush per-call cost should drop to microseconds.

title: Decide readiness semantics during a long write (readiness currently flaps)
description:
read_status uses try_read and maps TryLockError::WouldBlock to 503 (src/server/mod.rs:484-492). The reasoning in the doc comment is sound and deliberate: a probe must not block behind a long write, because a blocking acquisition would stall executor threads under a probe storm.

But /ready calls read_status (src/server/mod.rs:428), so the CONSEQUENCE is that any write long enough to span a readiness probe interval makes the instance report NOT READY — and Kubernetes removes it from the Service.

For a cluster WRITER that is self-harm at the worst moment: there is exactly one writer, it is doing exactly the work it exists to do (a large upsert), and readiness failing pulls it out of rotation mid-batch, so the writes that follow have nowhere to go. The instance is not unhealthy; it is BUSY. Those are different things and the readiness signal currently conflates them.

Note the interaction with the fix for nidus-lp4.1: 'busy' returning 503 was harmless when readiness meant only 'is a store open', and became load-bearing once readiness started gating traffic on fenced/stale state. This is a second-order effect of that change rather than a defect in it.

Also note it composes badly with nidus-abx.2: under load shedding, a busy instance would report both 'shed your request' AND 'I am not ready', so an orchestrator sees a flapping endpoint instead of a saturated one.
design:
This is a product decision before it is a code change, which is why it is filed as its own item rather than folded into nidus-abx.2.

The question: should "the store lock is momentarily held" make an instance NOT READY?

Recommended answer: NO. Readiness should mean "this instance can usefully serve" — open, not fenced, not stale. Busy is not one of those; it is what backpressure (nidus-abx.2) is for, and 503-on-shed already tells the client to retry without lying about the instance's health.

Implementation sketch, if that answer is accepted: the readiness-relevant facts (open, fenced, staleness) are all cheap ATOMIC or Instant reads on Store — Store::fenced is already an Arc<AtomicBool> after nidus-lp4.7, and AppState::open is already an AtomicBool. So readiness can be answered WITHOUT taking the store lock at all, which removes the WouldBlock case from the readiness path entirely and keeps the non-blocking property the current design rightly insists on. That likely means exposing those two or three fields separately from the full ClusterStatus rather than routing readiness through read_status.

Keep the WouldBlock -> 503 behaviour for /cluster and /stats, where "momentarily unable to answer" genuinely is the honest response and nothing routes on it.
acceptance_criteria: A long-running write does not make an otherwise-healthy instance report NOT ready; readiness still reports 503 for not-open, fenced, and stale; the readiness path takes no blocking lock; and an e2e test asserts readiness holds steady across an upsert long enough to span several probe intervals.
notes:
DECIDED (user, 2026-07-25): busy is NOT unready. Readiness must mean "this instance can usefully serve" — open, not fenced, not stale — and must not report NOT ready merely because the store lock is momentarily held.

Implement as sketched in the design: answer readiness from the cheap atomic/Instant reads only (Store::fenced is already an Arc<AtomicBool> after nidus-lp4.7, AppState::open is already an AtomicBool), so the readiness path takes NO blocking lock and the WouldBlock case disappears from it entirely.

Keep WouldBlock -> 503 for /cluster and /stats, where "momentarily unable to answer" is the honest response and nothing routes on it.

Related decision recorded on nidus-abx.1: liveness makes the same distinction in the other direction — a POISONED lock is unhealthy (restart me), a merely BUSY one is not. The two issues should end up consistent, and nidus-abx.7 (the stale doc comment on this same function) should be folded in here rather than fixed separately.
close_reason:
FIXED (v0.34.0). Readiness is answered from atomics only, via a new lock-free Readiness handle (Store::readiness / Nidus::readiness) published into a OnceLock when the store opens. The WouldBlock case is gone from the readiness path rather than tolerated. Store::last_verified became an Arc<AtomicU64> of monotonic millis so staleness is readable without the lock — deliberately monotonic, not SystemTime, since a backwards clock jump would make a reader look younger than it is.

/cluster and /stats keep WouldBlock -> 503: nothing routes on them, so 'momentarily unable to answer' is honest there. The contrast is asserted in the test.

Tests: a_busy_store_is_still_ready (in-process, deterministic — holds the write guard directly) and a_long_write_does_not_make_the_instance_report_unready (real binary, real socket, 10k-record upsert, with a guard assertion so it cannot silently pass by finishing too fast). Both verified to FAIL against the old lock-taking path.

title: No backpressure: no request timeout, concurrency limit, or load shedding
description:
The entire middleware stack is two layers (src/server/mod.rs:339-340):

    .layer(DefaultBodyLimit::max(max_body_bytes))
    .layer(middleware::from_fn_with_state(state.clone(), auth))

That bounds how big ONE request can be. Nothing bounds how MANY, or how LONG.

Consequences, all reachable from ordinary client behaviour rather than malice:

  * NO REQUEST TIMEOUT. A search over a large store is CPU-bound brute-force cosine (that is the design), executed on a blocking task while holding the store read lock. A client that disconnects mid-request does not cancel it — axum drops the response future, but the spawn_blocking work continues to completion. So abandoned work still costs a full scan.
  * NO CONCURRENCY LIMIT AND NO LOAD SHED. Every accepted request that needs the store queues on the RwLock. Under a client storm, in-flight request bodies (each up to max_body_bytes) accumulate in RAM on a store whose whole design is 'the working set is in RAM' — so the queue competes for memory with the data. There is no point at which the server says 'too much, go away'; it simply degrades until the allocator or the OOM killer intervenes. Note the library defends its OWN allocations with try_reserve (SPEC §6.6) — a deliberate, careful invariant — but that guard is bypassed by unbounded request queueing above it.
  * A LONG WRITE SERIALISES EVERYTHING. upsert takes the write lock for the whole batch. With no timeout, readers queue behind it indefinitely rather than failing fast; from a client's perspective the server has hung. This is also what drives the readiness flap in nidus-abx.3, which is why these two should be decided together.

tower 0.5 is ALREADY a dependency (Cargo.toml:160) so this needs feature flags, not a new crate — cheap in build-and-ship terms, which is the bar CLAUDE.md sets.
design:
Compose the standard tower layers, all configurable via ServeConfig + CLI flags with sane defaults (nidus's convention: every knob a flag, defaults that suit a single node):

  * TimeoutLayer — bound per-request wall time. Default must exceed a legitimate large upsert, so it is NOT a small number; consider separate bounds for read vs write routes, since their honest latencies differ by orders of magnitude.
  * ConcurrencyLimitLayer + LoadShedLayer — cap in-flight requests and return 503 beyond it rather than queueing. 503-with-Retry-After is the honest answer and composes with the readiness signal an orchestrator already reads.
  * Consider GlobalConcurrencyLimit tuned to the thread pool rather than a fixed number: search is CPU-bound, so admitting far more concurrent scans than cores buys nothing and costs memory.

Do NOT add per-IP rate limiting — that belongs at the proxy (see nidus-abx.7), and duplicating it here would be the wrong layer.

Measure before defaulting: benchmarks/ has the HTTP path (nidus-8fn measured ~100-140us constant overhead per query), so the timeout default can be grounded in real numbers rather than guessed. Deliberately note that cancellation of in-flight spawn_blocking work is NOT solved by a timeout layer (the timeout frees the CLIENT, not the CPU); genuinely cancelling a running scan would need a cooperative check in the scan loop and is a separate, larger decision — record it, do not silently imply it is fixed.
acceptance_criteria: Concurrent load beyond a configured limit is shed with 503 rather than queued; a request cannot occupy a connection indefinitely; the limits are configurable flags with documented defaults grounded in benchmark numbers; and the docs state plainly that a shed request is a retryable 503. An e2e test drives more concurrent requests than the limit and asserts 503s rather than unbounded latency.
notes:
DECIDED (implementation, 2026-07-25): hand-rolled `from_fn` middleware in src/server/limits.rs, NOT tower's ConcurrencyLimitLayer/LoadShedLayer/TimeoutLayer. Three reasons, in order of weight:

1. PROBES MUST NOT BE SHED. /health, /ready and /metrics have to answer while the instance is saturated — that is exactly when someone is looking. A tower layer wrapping the Router sheds uniformly, so a load spike would fail liveness and get a busy-but-healthy instance RESTARTED: the same availability trap nidus-abx.1/.3 just closed, reopened one layer up. Exempting paths needs a filter on the request, which is what the middleware is.
2. ConcurrencyLimitLayer's permit pool is per-clone and axum clones the router per connection, so the honest composition is GlobalConcurrencyLimitLayer — at which point the shared Semaphore in AppState is the same object with less indirection.
3. The response is the product: a shed request carries Retry-After + {"retryable": true}; tower surfaces Overloaded/Elapsed as errors HandleErrorLayer must downcast and re-dress.

Net: no new tower features enabled, no new dependency.

SHIPPED
- --max-concurrent-requests (0 = auto: 8x cores, floored at 64), --read-timeout (30s), --write-timeout (600s); 0 disables a timeout. All with NIDUS_* env vars and chart values.
- Read/write split by route: search-shaped POSTs (/search, /text-search, /hybrid-search, /list, */recall) classified as reads; every other mutating method defaults to the write bound (safe direction — a new mutating route is not cut off mid-batch).
- Shed = 503 + Retry-After: 1 + {"retryable": true}. Deadline = 504 + {"retryable": false} (the work MAY still be running; an immediate retry doubles it).
- Layer order: body limit (inner) -> backpressure -> auth -> observe (outer). Auth outside backpressure so an unauthenticated request never consumes a permit; observe outermost so 401s and shed 503s are counted.

RECORDED, NOT FIXED (as the issue asked): a timeout frees the CLIENT, not the CPU — spawn_blocking work is not cancellable, so an abandoned scan runs to completion. Consequence stated in limits.rs: the permit is released at the deadline, so the admission count understates in-flight work during an abandoned request's tail. Holding it would be worse (shedding live traffic for work nobody awaits). Genuinely cancelling a scan needs a cooperative check in the scan loop — separate, larger decision.

Defaults are grounded, not guessed: 8x cores because search is CPU-bound brute force (more concurrent scans than cores buys no throughput, costs memory), floored at 64 so a small container does not shed on trivial load. No per-IP rate limiting — documented as the proxy's job.

TESTS: unit (route classification, auto-resolution floor, permit fill/drain) + router-level (shed 503 + Retry-After, probes survive saturation, 504 on deadline then recovery) + e2e tests/e2e/hardening.rs (16 concurrent clients vs --max-concurrent-requests 1, paced to avoid exhausting the CLIENT's ephemeral ports, asserts 503s + server's own shed counter agrees).
close_reason: Closed

title: [BUG] A panicking handler bricks the instance permanently while /health still reports ok
description:
The store is held behind std::sync::RwLock (src/server/mod.rs:92, Arc<RwLock<Option<Nidus>>>). std's RwLock POISONS on a panic while the lock is held, and poisoning is permanent for the life of the process.

The code does notice: read_status maps TryLockError::Poisoned to a 500 'store lock poisoned' (src/server/mod.rs:493-495), and the handler helpers map it likewise (src/server/mod.rs:883-884, :902-903). So the failure is reported honestly per-request.

The problem is what happens NEXT: nothing recovers, and nothing escalates.

  * Every subsequent request 500s forever — the store is unreachable even though the process is fine and the data on disk is intact.
  * /health returns a HARDCODED "ok" (src/server/mod.rs:408-410), so a Kubernetes LIVENESS probe never fires and the pod is never restarted.
  * /ready calls read_status, so it WILL surface the 500 — but readiness only removes the pod from the Service. It does not restart it. The pod sits there, out of rotation, doing nothing, forever.

So a single panic in any handler converts an instance into a permanently dead-but-live pod that no probe will recycle. In a cluster that is worse than a crash: a crashed writer's lease lapses and a standby is promoted within lock_ttl (nidus-lp4.3), whereas a POISONED writer keeps its lease alive — the background renewal timer holds its own Drop-free LeaseRenewer and does not touch the store lock (by design, nidus-lp4.7) — so it goes on renewing a lease it can no longer use, and no standby is ever promoted. That is a cluster-wide write outage from one panic, with every signal saying the writer is alive and holding the handle.

Note this is not hypothetical-only: forbid(unsafe_code) does not prevent panics. Any index-out-of-bounds, unwrap, arithmetic overflow in debug, or allocation failure inside a handler reaches this state.
design:
Make /health report unhealthy when the store lock is poisoned, so a Kubernetes liveness probe restarts the pod. This is the same lesson as nidus-lp4.1 — a probe that cannot see a broken instance is an inverted signal — applied to LIVENESS rather than readiness.

Constraints:

  * Keep the health path non-blocking and cheap. Use try_read and treat only TryLockError::Poisoned as unhealthy; WouldBlock (merely busy) must stay healthy, or a long write would trigger a restart, which is a far worse bug than the one being fixed. Note this is the same busy-is-not-broken distinction that nidus-abx.3 makes for readiness.
  * /health currently returns a hardcoded &'static str (src/server/mod.rs:408-410) and is deliberately exempt from auth (src/server/mod.rs:351). Keep both properties: no token required, and no store lock acquired beyond the non-blocking poison check.
  * Do NOT clear the poison, and do NOT add a panic-catching layer — see the DECIDED note. The instance is meant to die and be replaced.
  * Readiness already surfaces the poison as a 500 via read_status, which is fine and needs no change; readiness removes the pod from the Service, liveness is what recycles it. Both signals should agree.

Test it by panicking a handler on purpose. Options: a test-only route behind #[cfg(test)] or a debug assertion reachable with a crafted request; the e2e harness can then assert /health goes unhealthy and the process is still alive (so a supervisor restarts it rather than reporting it hung — mirrors the existing assertion style in fenced_writer_reports_unready).

Also add the cluster consequence to the docs: a poisoned writer reports unhealthy, gets restarted, its lease then lapses, and a --wait-for-lease standby is promoted within lock_ttl. That is the intended recovery path and it only works if liveness fires.
acceptance_criteria: A panic in any handler cannot leave the instance permanently failing every request: either it never poisons the lock, or the process reports unhealthy on /health so a liveness probe restarts it. A cluster writer that reaches this state does not keep renewing a lease it cannot use while blocking standby promotion. Covered by a test that panics a handler on purpose and asserts the instance either recovers or reports unhealthy.
notes:
DECIDED (user, 2026-07-25): no new dependency. /health escalation is the fix; containment is explicitly NOT wanted.

Sharpened by an empirical check of std's semantics (run during triage, 2026-07-25): a panic while holding a READ guard does NOT poison an RwLock; only a panic while holding the WRITE guard does. Verified directly:

    after read-path panic  -> is_poisoned = false
    after write-path panic -> is_poisoned = true

That changes the shape of this issue for the better, and rules out the containment options originally sketched:

  * Poisoning can ONLY arise from a panic taken while the store was locked exclusively — that is, mid-mutation of the in-RAM index. So a poisoned store is, by construction, one whose in-RAM state may not match the durable bytes.
  * Therefore suppressing the poison is the WRONG move. RwLock::clear_poison would resume serving from a possibly-inconsistent index, and CatchPanicLayer (tower-http) would leave exactly the same inconsistent index behind while removing the one flag that says so. Both trade a loud, correct failure for a quiet, incorrect one.
  * The poison flag is therefore a USEFUL SIGNAL, not a problem to be papered over. The remedy is a restart, and the only thing missing is the escalation path that triggers one.
  * Bonus consequence: a panic on the READ path (a search) cannot brick the instance at all, so the whole failure mode is writer-only — which is consistent with the cluster analysis in the description (a poisoned writer keeps renewing its lease and blocks standby promotion).

So: tower-http is NOT needed, clear_poison is NOT to be used, and the scope shrinks to making /health honest.
close_reason:
FIXED (v0.34.0). /health now reports 503 when the store lock is poisoned, so liveness restarts the process. No new dependency: the empirical finding in the notes — std poisons only on a WRITE-path panic — ruled out both containment options, since a poisoned store is by construction one whose in-RAM index may not match the durable bytes. clear_poison and CatchPanicLayer would each resume serving from that suspect index; the poison flag is the useful signal and a restart is the remedy.

Readiness checks the same flag (is_poisoned acquires nothing, so it stays off the lock), because otherwise traffic keeps arriving for however long the liveness probe takes to fire. That gap was caught by a test, not by inspection: making readiness lock-free for nidus-abx.3 initially made it blind to poisoning.

Tests: a_poisoned_store_lock_reports_unhealthy_so_liveness_restarts_it, plus a_panic_on_the_read_path_leaves_the_instance_healthy which pins the std semantics the design rests on — if read-path panics ever started poisoning, health would begin firing on harmless search panics.

title: Harden the serving edge for production
description:
Cluster mode's coordination layer is now solid: the writer lease is CAS-acquired, CAS-renewed, truncation-safe, and fenced, with honest readiness and lease observability (epic nidus-lp4, closed 2026-07-25 at v0.33.0). Production risk has therefore MOVED — it is no longer in the lease protocol but at the SERVING EDGE: the HTTP layer has almost no middleware, no traffic-level observability, and no documented security posture.

Found by auditing src/server/mod.rs against main at 03b01ba (v0.33.0). Every item below carries file:line evidence and was verified against the code, not inferred. None of it was in the tracker — the only filed work remaining was the JS SDK epic, which is client convenience, not server hardening.

The through-line: nidus's LIBRARY invariants are carefully defended (rollback on partial write, try_reserve for OOM, CAS fencing, forbid(unsafe_code)) but the SERVER wrapping them has two tower layers total — a body limit and auth. A production deployment's failure modes now live in that gap.

Ordering is by production impact: .1-.3 are availability traps that can take an instance or a cluster down; .4-.5 are what an on-call engineer needs to diagnose one; .6-.7 are security posture; .8 is housekeeping.
design:
Sequencing: .1 first (it is the only item that can leave a process permanently bricked while reporting healthy), then .2 (backpressure, which .3 interacts with), then .3 as an explicit product decision about readiness semantics. .4-.5 are independent and can land any time. .6-.7 should land together as one coherent security-posture change. .8 is a one-line fix that can ride along with anything.

Dependency note: tower 0.5 is ALREADY a dependency (Cargo.toml:160), so timeout / concurrency-limit / load-shed need only feature flags, not a new crate. Panic containment is the exception — CatchPanicLayer lives in tower-http, a new (pure-Rust, small) dependency, so per CLAUDE.md that is a design decision to raise rather than an implementation detail. .1 offers a dependency-free alternative.
acceptance_criteria: An instance cannot be left permanently failing while reporting healthy; the server sheds load rather than queueing unboundedly; readiness semantics during a long write are a decided, documented behaviour; traffic-level metrics and correlatable logs exist; and the TLS/token posture is explicit in the docs.
notes: DECIDED (user, 2026-07-25): nidus-abx.1 takes the /health-escalation route with NO new dependency (tower-http is not needed and clear_poison is not to be used — see that issue's notes for the std poisoning semantics that settle it). nidus-abx.3 takes 'busy is not unready', answering readiness from atomics with no lock on the path. Both decisions are recorded on the children; the epic's sequencing note stands.
close_reason: Closed

title: Standby writers: wait for the lease instead of crash-looping (bounded failover)
description:
THE availability gap — and the property leader election was actually wanted for.

Today src/backend/object.rs try_claim is single-shot: on contention it returns Ok(None), which Store::open_with turns into the 'store is locked' error, so a would-be standby writer EXITS IMMEDIATELY. Verified across real processes in tests/e2e/cluster.rs::second_writer_is_excluded_across_processes. charts/nidus/values.yaml:112 admits the consequence: 'Keep replicaCount at 1. With >1, the extra pods lose the lock race and crash-loop.'

So the de facto failover mechanism is an EXTERNAL supervisor restarting the writer until the lease goes stale and a restart happens to win (which is exactly what cluster::killed_writer_lease_is_taken_over_with_data_intact proves). Two problems: it is undocumented, and failover latency is lease TTL PLUS whatever backoff the supervisor has reached — Kubernetes exponential backoff climbs into minutes, and CrashLoopBackOff is an alert to an operator, not a design.

Shape: an opt-in wait/standby mode (e.g. Config::wait_for_lease(Duration) + --wait-for-lease) where a ReadWrite open RETRIES acquisition instead of failing. A standby then sits idle holding no lease and takes over within ~lease TTL of the incumbent dying, making failover bounded and observable rather than emergent. No coordinator, no consensus, no new failure domain — it only changes what a writer does when it finds the lease held.

Design notes:
- Standbys must serve nothing while waiting, or they would answer requests against an unopened store — so decide explicitly whether the HTTP listener binds before or after acquisition. Binding first with a not-ready readiness (nidus-lp4.1) is probably right, so a standby is addressable and visibly not-ready rather than invisible.
- Retry needs jitter: N standbys waking simultaneously on TTL expiry would thunder at the lock object.
- Must compose with nidus-lp4.1 so a standby reports unready while waiting and ready once promoted.
- e2e test to add in tests/e2e/cluster.rs: start writer + standby, SIGKILL the writer, assert the standby is serving writes within ~TTL WITHOUT any external restart — the assertion that is impossible today.
acceptance_criteria: A standby writer process started while the lease is held stays up, and takes over within ~lock_ttl of the incumbent being SIGKILLed, with no external restart; asserted end-to-end across real processes.
notes:
IMPLEMENTED on branch cluster-standby-promotion (stacked on PR #56, v0.31.0, chart 0.3.0).

LIBRARY: Config::lease_wait + LeaseWait { Fail (default — unchanged fail-fast), Timeout(d), Forever }. Store::await_writer_handle wraps BOTH acquisition paths (cluster ClusterLease::acquire and the plain lock) at the single existing choke point; retries at lock_ttl/8 clamped to [250ms, 2s] with up to +25% jitter (several standbys would otherwise wake in lockstep on TTL expiry and stampede the lock object). Correctness unchanged — the conditional write still makes exactly one claimant win, so retrying adds no race.

CLI: --wait-for-lease with clap num_args(0..=1) + default_missing_value, so bare = Forever and a number = Timeout(secs); non-numeric is a clear error.

SERVER (the part that makes it real, not theoretical): serve() now takes an OPENER CLOSURE and BINDS BEFORE OPENING. A standby that isn't listening fails its liveness probe, so a supervisor kills exactly the instance meant to be waiting. Split the probes accordingly: /health = alive (answers throughout the wait), /ready = store open (503 while waiting). Data routes 503 not 500 while unopened. Both probes auth-exempt (an orchestrator reads 401 as not-ready). /ready reads an AtomicBool, NOT the store lock — a probe must be constant-time, and a blocking read behind a multi-second upsert would stall probes and eventually async executor threads.

CAUGHT BY THE EXISTING E2E SUITE: /health no longer implies 'store open', so the harness's readiness wait had to move to /ready — 10 tests failed until it did. Good regression signal.

VERIFIED against real minio+valkey: 'standby promoted 1.86s after the writer was killed' with lock_ttl=2, NO external restart. New test standby_is_promoted_after_the_writer_dies also pins: waiting standby is live but not ready, its data routes 503, promotion is unattended, and the promoted instance inherits committed data. 18/18 e2e, 495 lib tests, docs + helm lint + kubeconform all green.

CHART: readinessProbe -> /ready; new nidus.cluster / waitForLease / lockTtl values; removed the now-false 'cluster mode is not yet exposed by the server' and the replicaCount>1-crash-loops warning (>1 is now supported WITH waitForLease). Recreate stays the default updateStrategy but the comment notes RollingUpdate becomes viable with standbys.

NOT covered here (still nidus-lp4.1): /ready reports only whether the store is OPEN — a FENCED writer and an arbitrarily STALE reader both still report ready. That is the remaining production gap in the probe story.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #57 (--wait-for-lease standby promotion), verified by e2e standby_is_promoted_after_the_writer_dies. Now safe to recommend: the mutual-exclusion break that blocked it (nidus-lp4.7) is fixed.

title: Cluster mode must refuse a backend without compare-and-swap
description:
Cluster mode currently accepts a persistence backend with no CAS primitive and silently degrades to ADVISORY locking. src/store/mod.rs:225 and :637 branch on has_native_lock(), falling back to a best-effort get-then-put (src/backend/object.rs try_claim -> advisory_claim), and SPEC §14.6 documents this as 'a backend without CAS degrades to the per-batch lease fence alone'.

Advisory locking means two writers CAN both believe they hold the lease, and the mid-batch fence that CAS provides is simply absent — so split-brain and clobbered commits are possible. That is an acceptable trade for a single-node advisory lock; it is not acceptable for cluster mode, whose entire safety argument rests on the conditional write.

Fix: in cluster mode, refuse at open() unless the resolved backend advertises CAS — the same class of guard as the existing 'cluster mode requires a shared object-store persistence backend' and '... requires a shared memory tier' errors, which are already clear and well-tested. Non-cluster single-writer use keeps the advisory fallback unchanged.

Note GCS: src/backend/gcs.rs:291 try_lock returns Ok(None) with has_native_lock() false, yet gcs DOES implement put_cas via ifGenerationMatch — so verify which capability the guard should key on (CAS support, not try_lock support), or GCS would be wrongly rejected.
acceptance_criteria: Opening a cluster store on a non-CAS backend fails with a clear, actionable error naming the missing capability; S3 and GCS both still open; single-node advisory locking is unaffected.
notes: IMPLEMENTED on branch cluster-hardening (v0.32.0, chart 0.4.0). See the commit for detail; verified by new e2e tests against real minio+valkey.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #58 (v0.32.0): open() refuses cluster mode unless persistence.supports_cas(). Keyed on CAS support, not try_lock, so GCS is correctly accepted. Verified by e2e cluster_mode_is_refused_without_the_required_backends.

title: /health lies: a fenced writer and an arbitrarily stale reader both report ok
description:
src/server/mod.rs:216 is 'async fn health() -> &'static str { "ok" }' — a hardcoded string that never touches the store. charts/nidus/values.yaml:146 and :154 wire BOTH the liveness and readiness probes to it.

Consequences in the SHIPPED chart:
1. A writer that has been FENCED (superseded, lease lost) reports healthy, stays in the Service endpoints, and keeps receiving writes that every single one of which will fail with 'writer lease lost'. The one signal Kubernetes could act on is inverted.
2. An arbitrarily stale read-only instance reports healthy with no staleness bound (refresh is manual — see nidus-lp4.4).
3. Liveness and readiness share one endpoint, so they cannot mean different things — but they must: a fenced writer is UNREADY (pull it from the LB) yet arguably still LIVE (restarting it is in fact the current failover mechanism).

Shape: /health grows a real check, and readiness and liveness need to diverge. Suggested — /health stays a liveness probe (process is up, store is open) and a new /ready reflects role state: a cluster writer that has lost its lease is NOT ready; a reader past a configured staleness bound is NOT ready. Keep /health's current auth exemption. Then split the chart's probes.

Care needed: readiness must not require a lock or an object-store round trip on every probe (every 5s per pod) — read cached lease state, do not re-fetch the manifest.

Found while answering 'how are we handling election and failover' (2026-07-25).
acceptance_criteria: A fenced cluster writer fails its readiness probe and leaves the Service endpoints; a reader past its staleness bound does too; liveness and readiness are separate endpoints with separate chart probes; no probe performs object-store IO.
notes:
PARTIALLY UNBLOCKED by nidus-lp4.3 (branch cluster-standby-promotion): /ready now exists as a separate endpoint from /health, reads a lock-free AtomicBool, is auth-exempt, and the chart's readinessProbe points at it. So the endpoint split and the probe wiring — items this issue called for — are DONE.

REMAINING, and still the substance of this issue: /ready reports only 'is the store open'. A cluster writer that has been FENCED still reports ready (its every write fails with 'writer lease lost'), and a reader that is arbitrarily STALE still reports ready. Both need the readiness check to consult role state — and must keep doing so without object-store IO or taking the store lock (the AtomicBool pattern lp4.3 established is the model).
IMPLEMENTED on branch cluster-hardening (v0.32.0, chart 0.4.0). See the commit for detail; verified by new e2e tests against real minio+valkey.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #58 (v0.32.0), verified green by tests/e2e/cluster.rs::fenced_writer_reports_unready and stale_reader_reports_unready. Was left open only because the bd status was never updated when the branch merged.

title: Harden cluster mode for production use
description:
Cluster mode's SAFETY is solid and now verified against real S3 (nidus-1e6.3): a per-batch-renewed writer lease plus compare-and-swap on every durable write, with a SIGSTOP-stalled writer provably unable to clobber its successor. What is missing is AVAILABILITY and OPERABILITY — the parts an on-call engineer needs.

OPEN PRODUCT DECISION (user raised 2026-07-25): whether to add real leader election / a coordinator. Recorded here rather than dropped, because SPEC §14.6 currently says 'not a managed cluster — no coordinator, replication, or rebalancing' and the user questions whether that survives a production goal.

The argument against a self-hosted quorum, for whoever decides: nidus ALREADY has a coordinator — the object store. S3 If-Match / GCS ifGenerationMatch are linearizable compare-and-swap, which is exactly the primitive election needs, and is why the existing fencing works. Same design as Delta Lake / Iceberg commit protocols and Kubernetes leases over etcd. Adding Raft would (a) require instance-to-instance networking, of which nidus has NONE today, (b) add a second source of truth that can disagree with the object store, (c) make 3 instances the safety minimum where 1 writer + N readers works now, and (d) STILL need the CAS fence, since a Raft leader can be stale w.r.t. the store. So 'no coordinator' is best read as 'no coordinator of our own', not 'no linearizable authority'.

If that reading is accepted, nidus-1e6-hard.3 (standby writers waiting on the lease) delivers the availability property election was wanted for — bounded promotion ≈ lease TTL — with no new failure domain. If it is rejected, election becomes a separate epic and this one is still a prerequisite.

Children are ordered by production impact, NOT by the election question: .1 and .2 are outright bugs that matter under any decision.
design: Sequencing: .1 and .2 first (they are correctness/safety bugs in shipped artifacts), then .3 (the availability gap), then .4-.6 (operability). Each is additive; none requires the election decision to be settled.
notes:
DECIDED (user, 2026-07-25): NO coordinator / no consensus protocol. The object store's compare-and-swap (S3 If-Match, GCS ifGenerationMatch) is accepted as the linearizable authority, so SPEC §14.6's 'no coordinator' stance stands — a self-hosted quorum would add instance-to-instance networking nidus does not have, a second source of truth that can disagree with the store, a 3-instance safety minimum, and would still need the CAS fence anyway. Election is NOT to be built. The availability property it was wanted for comes from nidus-lp4.3 (standby writers waiting on the lease) instead. This closes the open product decision recorded above.
Epic implemented on branch cluster-hardening (v0.32.0): lp4.1, .2, .4, .5 done; .3 done earlier on PR #57; .6 PARTIAL. The epic surfaced two lease bugs — one fixed (Clone-on-owning-guard released the lease), one OPEN and P0 (nidus-lp4.6b: a standby acquires while the incumbent is healthy, so two instances both report holds_writer_handle). Do not advertise --wait-for-lease as production-ready until lp4.6b is resolved.
close_reason: All 7 children complete. Cluster mode is production-hardened: honest readiness (/ready reports fenced + stale), CAS required at open, standby promotion via --wait-for-lease, reader staleness exposed and bounded, lease observability on /cluster, out-of-band lease renewal, and the lease protocol itself corrected (nidus-lp4.7: CAS-gated renewal, truncation-safe staleness, transient-vs-permanent failure classification, background fence latching). --wait-for-lease is now safe to recommend. The 'no coordinator' decision stands: the object store's compare-and-swap is the linearizable authority.

title: benchmarks crate did not compile — Record.vector -> Option<Vec<f32>> broke every target
description:
Found while adding the server engine (nidus-8fn). The whole nidus-bench crate failed to compile: Record.vector became Option<Vec<f32>> when FTS introduced text-only records, and no benchmark site was updated — engines/nidus.rs:42, src/quant.rs:105, src/ann.rs:202, and benches/nidus_regression.rs:27 + :137.

Consequence: 'just bench', 'just bench-quant' and 'just bench-ann' were ALL dead, so no performance or recall claim about nidus was verifiable for however long this sat.

ROOT CAUSE of it going unnoticed: Cargo.toml has default-members = ["."], so neither 'cargo test' nor any CI lane ever compiles nidus-bench. That default is correct — it is what keeps the core build seconds-long — so the fix is NOT to change it and slow every local test run.

FIXED (v0.30.0, branch e2e-server-harness): wrapped all 5 sites in Some(...), plus a new ci.yml job 'bench-compiles' running 'cargo clippy -p nidus-bench --all-targets --features server -- -D warnings'. Build only, never run: benchmark timings on a shared runner are meaningless. duckdb/lancedb stay excluded — bundled C++ and Arrow+DataFusion are the multi-minute compiles nidus exists to avoid, and are opt-in for a human comparing engines.

Verified: all bench targets compile and clippy clean; 'just bench-server' produces real numbers.
acceptance_criteria: nidus-bench compiles on every PR; just bench/bench-quant/bench-ann all run.
close_reason: Fixed in the same change that found it (v0.30.0, PR #56): all 5 sites wrapped in Some(...), and a new ci.yml 'bench-compiles' job clippies -p nidus-bench --all-targets --features server with -D warnings so it cannot rot again. Verified: every bench target compiles, clippy clean, and just bench-server produces real numbers.

title: E2E: scale + ranking-correctness suite (10k x 384-d through HTTP vs ground truth)
description:
The e2e suite proved the wire protocol and process behaviour but used dim=3 with 2-6 hand-picked orthogonal vectors, so it said nothing about whether RANKING IS CORRECT over a realistic corpus, nor what the server costs. benchmarks/ does cover realistic scale + recall@k, but every cell drives Nidus IN-PROCESS (build_store -> Nidus::open_in_memory), so the HTTP path — JSON-encoding hundreds of floats per request, the Arc<RwLock> + spawn_blocking hop, socket framing — was measured nowhere. A serialization regression could 10x server latency with nothing noticing.

IMPLEMENTED (tests/e2e/scale.rs, 3 tests, NOT ignored — ~2s each, run on every PR):
1. exact_search_at_scale_matches_ground_truth — 10k x 384-d ingested in 500-record batches over HTTP, then top-10 compared against cosine ground truth computed INDEPENDENTLY in-test (SplitMix64 seeded generator, no new dep). Asserts the full ranking id-for-id AND the scores within 1e-4, so a normalisation bug that preserved rank order would still fail.
2. filtered_search_at_scale_matches_ground_truth — a predicate admitting 1/10 of rows; asserts the filtered ranking matches ground truth AND that every hit genuinely satisfies the predicate (a leaking filter would still rank plausibly).
3. quantized_search_at_scale_keeps_high_recall — int8 first pass + f32 rerank end-to-end; asserts mean recall@10 >= 0.8 (a floor against 'quantization returns noise', not a recall tracker).

MEASURED (debug build, local): ingest 10k x 384-d in 2.72s (3675 vec/s) over HTTP; worst query 43ms; int8 recall@10 = 1.000.

PERF ASSERTIONS ARE DELIBERATELY ORDER-OF-MAGNITUDE (user's call): these run in a DEBUG build on shared CI runners, so tight bounds would flake and absolute numbers are meaningless. Ceilings are ~100x the measured values (query < 5s, ingest < 120s) — they catch 'someone made search quadratic', not a 20% regression. Real perf tracking stays in benchmarks/ (--release). Measured values are always printed so CI logs carry the trend.

VERIFIED NOT VACUOUS: reversing the expected ranking makes the test fail with the two lists as exact reverses, proving the server returned precisely the independently-computed order.
acceptance_criteria: Exact search over 10k x 384-d through HTTP reproduces independently-computed ground truth (ids + scores); filtered and quantized paths asserted; runs on every PR without flaking.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #56: tests/e2e/scale.rs ingests 10k x 384-d over HTTP and checks top-k against cosine ground truth computed in-test, across exact, filtered and quantized paths. 3 tests green. Timing assertions kept order-of-magnitude only (debug build, shared runner).

title: serve --cluster --read-only never refreshes: readers serve a frozen snapshot forever
description:
Found by the phase-2 multi-process e2e work (nidus-1e6.3), against real minio + valkey.

Nidus::refresh() (src/lib.rs:323) exists and is well covered at the library level, but src/server/ NEVER CALLS IT and exposes no route to trigger it (grep for 'refresh' in src/server/ and src/cli/ returns nothing). So a 'nidus serve --cluster --read-only' reader adopts the writer's state once at open() and then serves that snapshot forever.

REPRODUCED (writer + reader processes, shared s3://minio bucket + valkey tier):
  reader doc_count at open:        1   (correct — open-time adoption works)
  writer upserts a 2nd record:    2
  reader after the commit (+3s):   1   (never updates)

This makes cluster mode effectively non-functional for its headline purpose — fanning reads out across instances over one writer's data — even though every underlying piece (lease, CAS, manifest commit counter, refresh, tier adopt) works. The in-process cluster tests in src/store/tests.rs call store.refresh() directly, which is precisely why they never surfaced this: nothing proved the SERVER does.

Blocks the 'reader sees the writer's commits' assertion in nidus-1e6.3; the rest of that suite (writer exclusion, SIGKILL fencing/takeover, CAS against real S3, fresh-open adoption) is independent and proceeds.

Design fork for whoever picks this up — the options differ in cost, not just code: (a) an explicit POST /refresh route, client-driven, no policy baked in; (b) refresh automatically before each read when cluster+ReadOnly, correct by default but adds a manifest GET per request (latency + per-request object-store cost); (c) (b) with a staleness bound so at most one refresh per N ms, bounding the cost but adding a tunable.
acceptance_criteria: A reader process serving --cluster --read-only observes a writer process's commits; the e2e assertion in nidus-1e6.3 passes unignored.
close_reason: Fixed on branch e2e-server-harness (v0.30.0): POST /refresh route (src/server/mod.rs) calls Nidus::refresh() and returns {"adopted": bool} so a poller can tell 'advanced' from 'no change'. Explicit rather than auto-refresh-on-read (user's call): refreshing before every read would put a manifest GET on the hot path of exactly the read-heavy fan-out cluster mode exists for. Safe in every mode — refresh() already returns Ok(false) for writers and in-memory stores, so no mode-gating needed. Covered by refresh_is_a_no_op_without_a_shared_writer (in-process) + cluster::reader_adopts_writer_commits_on_refresh (two real processes over minio+valkey, asserting the reader is stale BEFORE the refresh and current after). Documented in the HTTP API reference + the CLI guide's cluster section, both of which now state the staleness contract explicitly.

title: Phase 3: .github/workflows/integration.yml — blocking PR check with minio + valkey services
description:
Its OWN workflow file (per user decision — NOT folded into ci.yml, which today has no services: block anywhere). Runs on pull_request + push to main, and is a REQUIRED/BLOCKING status check: it must pass to merge.

Shape, modeled on the existing ci.yml jobs (actions/checkout@v6, dtolnay/rust-toolchain@stable, actions/cache@v5 keyed like the matrix job at ci.yml:94):
- services: minio (health-checked on /minio/health/live) + valkey (redis-cli ping), both with GH-Actions health checks so the suite never races container startup — the #1 source of flaky integration CI.
- a step to mb the bucket before the suite (minio starts empty).
- env: AWS_ENDPOINT_URL / AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID / AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY / AWS_REGION pointing at the service, NIDUS_* as needed.
- cargo build --features cli FIRST (the harness spawns the built binary, so build failures surface as build failures, not confusing spawn timeouts), then just test-e2e (which runs the #[ignore]d suite via --ignored).
- a sane job timeout-minutes and, on failure, dump the child stdout/stderr the harness captured so a red PR is diagnosable without a rerun.

Do NOT add these deps or docker to the default lanes: 'just test' / 'just ci' stay pure-library and seconds-long, and the build-under-one-minute guard (build-thesis job, ci.yml:119) is untouched.

Finally: mark the job required in branch protection (needs a repo-settings change, not just the YAML — call it out in the PR description so it actually gets flipped, otherwise the check is advisory and the whole point is lost).
acceptance_criteria: integration.yml green on its own PR; job is listed as a required check in branch protection; ci.yml default lanes unchanged and still fast; a deliberately-broken e2e test makes the PR red.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #56: .github/workflows/integration.yml brings up minio + valkey via the shared scripts/e2e-services.sh and runs 'cargo test --features cli --test e2e -- --include-ignored' on every PR. NOTE: whether it is a *required* status check is a GitHub branch-protection setting, not verifiable from the tree — confirm in repo settings.

title: Phase 2: multi-process cluster e2e over real minio (S3) + valkey (memory tier)
description:
The half that today has no analogue at all: two or more REAL nidus serve processes over a SHARED real object store and a SHARED real Redis-family tier. Existing cluster tests are one process, two Store values, InMemObjectStore + LocalRam.

No product code needed for the backends — src/backend/s3.rs:75-84 already routes a custom AWS_ENDPOINT_URL path-style explicitly for MinIO/localstack, and the tier takes a valkey:// URL. So the harness just sets AWS_ENDPOINT_URL / AWS_ACCESS_KEY_ID / AWS_SECRET_ACCESS_KEY / AWS_REGION on the spawned children and passes --persistence s3://bucket/store --memory valkey://... --cluster.

Suite (all #[ignore]d — they need docker; CI runs them via just test-e2e): (1) writer + reader across PROCESS boundaries — writer upserts, reader (--read-only) refresh()es and serves the new rows; asserts the manifest commit-counter path works over a real object store, not a RAM mock. (2) writer exclusion — a second --cluster writer is refused while the lease is held. (3) HARD fencing — SIGKILL the writer (no drop, no clean release, no lock file cleanup — the case drop(first) can never simulate), then assert a new writer takes over after lock_ttl and that committed data survived. (4) CAS fencing against a REAL store — the paused-mid-batch superseded writer is REFUSED by If-Match rather than clobbering; verifies real S3 ETag semantics match what InMemObjectStore models (the actual risk nidus-ahw item 2 flags). (5) valkey tier adopt — a fresh reader adopts the shared working-set snapshot instead of replaying the log. (6) optionally run one leg against a Valkey CLUSTER container to exercise the slot-routing/MOVED path (nidus-wl1 shipped it; never tested against a real cluster).

Closes most of nidus-ahw item 2 — its 'cannot run cloud in dev env' blocker dissolves with minio. Update that issue rather than duplicating it.
acceptance_criteria: just test-e2e green against docker-run minio+valkey; SIGKILL takeover and CAS-refusal both asserted against real backends; nidus-ahw updated with what real-backend verification now covers vs what still needs an actual AWS/GCS bucket.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #56: tests/e2e/cluster.rs drives several real instances over real minio + valkey — cross-process exclusion, SIGSTOP fencing, killed-writer takeover, reader refresh. 14 tests green (incl. the two added in #59).

title: Phase 1: e2e harness + standalone-server suite against a real spawned binary
description:
New tests/e2e/ (gated: #![cfg(feature = "cli")]) with the reusable harness the whole epic + nidus-70x.2 build on: a ServerHandle that spawns the built binary via std::process::Command with --addr 127.0.0.1:0 over a tempfile::TempDir, parses the bound port from the phase-0 startup line, polls /health until ready with a timeout, exposes a ureq-based client (already a default dep — no new dev-dep), and kills + reaps the child on Drop so a failing assert never leaks a process.

Coverage this adds that oneshot() cannot: real TcpListener bind + axum::serve, the CLI-flag -> ServeConfig wiring, real HTTP framing over a socket, graceful shutdown (SIGTERM -> flush -> lock release), and the binary as shipped.

Suite: (1) full lifecycle create -> upsert -> search -> text-search -> hybrid -> stats, mirroring server/mod.rs full_lifecycle_over_http but over the wire; (2) --token auth — 401 without the bearer, 200 with it, /health exempt; (3) --max-body-bytes — an oversize upsert gets 413, not a hang or a panic; (4) concurrent clients — N threads issuing searches against one server, asserting no deadlock in the Arc<RwLock<Nidus>> + spawn_blocking path (untestable with oneshot); (5) restart durability — upsert, SIGTERM, respawn on the same dir, assert the data is there and the writer lock was released; (6) a second serve on the same dir fails with the friendly locked message (nidus-32y's fix, never verified against two real processes).

Mark #[ignore] only where genuinely slow; the local-FS server suite needs no docker and SHOULD run in the default cli lane. Add just recipe test-e2e.
acceptance_criteria: cargo test --features cli passes; no orphaned nidus processes after a forced failure; harness helper is reusable by phase 2 and mirrored by nidus-70x.2.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #56: tests/e2e/harness.rs spawns a real nidus serve on :0, learns the port from the startup line, polls /health, reaps on Drop; server.rs holds the assertions. 10 tests green.

title: Phase 0 (PREREQ): CLI flags for the library Config surface e2e needs — --cluster, --mmap, --quantization, …
description:
BLOCKS the cluster half of the epic outright. src/cli/mod.rs:158-165 builds Config with only .distance/.ann/.persistence/.memory/.open_mode — so 'nidus serve' can ONLY ever run the default exact brute-force, all-RAM, single-writer configuration. Every other Config builder is unreachable from the binary: cluster(), mmap(), quantization(), query_threads(), segment_max_rows(), segment_index_min_rows(), lock_ttl(), fsync(), auto_compact(), max_vector_bytes().

The blocker: with no --cluster flag you CANNOT start two serve processes in cluster mode, so phase 2 is untestable until this lands. The rest are the same class of gap and are cheap to add alongside.

Also fix here: serve() logs the REQUESTED address, not the bound one — src/server/mod.rs:104 eprintln!s cfg.addr, so '--addr 127.0.0.1:0' prints ':0' and neither a test harness nor a user can learn the real port. Print listener.local_addr() instead. One line, and it makes --addr :0 genuinely usable (the harness in phase 1 depends on it, and it avoids port-collision flakes without racy pick-a-free-port-and-drop).

Ship the flags with env fallbacks matching the existing NIDUS_* convention, and note that shipping quantization/mmap/query-threads flags means the Docker image and Helm chart can express those modes too.
acceptance_criteria: nidus serve --cluster works end to end; --addr 127.0.0.1:0 prints the actually-bound port; every added flag has an NIDUS_* env fallback; just ci-cli green; version bumped.
notes: IMPLEMENTED on branch cli-config-flags-and-bound-port (PR #55, v0.29.0). All missing store flags added with NIDUS_* env fallbacks: --cluster, --mmap, --quantization/--quant-rescore, --query-threads, --segment-max-rows, --segment-index-min-rows, --fsync, --auto-compact/--no-auto-compact, --lock-ttl, --max-vector-bytes. No new validation needed — existing store guards surface clearly (verified by hand: --cluster on local FS, and with s3:// but no memory tier, both refused by name). serve() now reports listener.local_addr() instead of cfg.addr, so --addr 127.0.0.1:0 prints the real port (verified: parsed 51513 from the startup line, /health answered ok) — this is the seam the phase-1 harness parses. StoreArgs derives Default, collapsing 3 test literals. Tests: store_flags_reach_config, store_flags_omitted_keep_config_defaults (guards against silently changing defaults), quantization_kinds_and_rescore_override, auto_compact_ratio_and_disable_conflict. Docs: 2 new sections in the CLI guide. just ci + ci-cli (490 tests) + docs build green. Left OPEN pending PR review.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #55 (aae19eb): CLI exposes the library Config surface (--cluster, --mmap, --quantization, --lock-ttl, …) and reports the actually-bound port. Verified by e2e opt_in_flags_reach_the_running_store.

title: E2E integration tests: real nidus serve process + real cluster over minio/valkey
description:

title: Atomic appends + batch rollback (data & log) — prevent ENOSPC corruption
description:

A process that catches the Err and keeps writing corrupts the store.

- src/data/mod.rs::append: capture pre-write offset (stream_position); on write_all error, set_len+seek back so a torn partial row never persists (atomic per row). New truncate_to(rows) batch-rollback primitive (file set_len to HEADER+rows*stride, seek, truncate vectors to rows*dim; works file+in-memory).
- src/log/mod.rs::append: same atomic treatment (roll back partial frame on failure). New offset()->u64 and truncate_to(offset) primitives.
- src/store/mod.rs::upsert becomes a transaction: capture data_mark=row_count & log_mark=offset; reserve up-front; append vectors (rollback data on err); sync data (rollback on err); append log ops (rollback log+data on err); sync log (rollback both); THEN commit to in-RAM index (infallible, capacity pre-reserved). Other log writers (delete/drop/set_meta/create_collection) rely on per-frame atomic append.
