title: Group commit: coalesce concurrent upserts into one fsync
description:
Option 1 from the nidus-xb9 decision, and the item with the most measured headroom behind it.

MEASURED BASIS (see the decision recorded on nidus-xb9, from just bench-write):
  * Per-upsert-call fixed cost is ~7.6ms, paid whether the call carries 1 record or 1000. Batch=1 gets 125 vec/s over HTTP; batch=1000 gets 33k. Same code.
  * A single serve process already has 2-8 upserts genuinely in flight at once — the concurrency sweep goes 33k -> 84k vec/s (384-d) as clients rise — and every one of them currently pays its OWN disk barrier.
  * The plateau (~84k/s at 384-d, ~67k/s at 768-d) sits on the in-process durable rate, so the exclusive write section IS the asymptote. Merging the barriers is how that asymptote moves.

SHAPE. A group-commit window: when a write is ready to sync and other writes are queued behind the lock, let them all append first and sync once for the group, acknowledging all of them after the single fsync. Classic WAL group commit. Every existing invariant holds — the ordering (data before log) is unchanged, and no request is acknowledged before its own bytes are durable; the only change is that N requests share one barrier instead of taking N.

Do nidus-4h2 FIRST. It removes an unconditional per-call data fsync, which changes the constant this optimisation is working against — measuring group commit on top of a doubled barrier cost would mis-size the window.

ACCEPTANCE
  * Concurrent upserts to one serve instance issue fewer fsyncs than upserts, measurably (a counter, or the barrier count in the bench).
  * No request returns 200 before its data is durable — a crash test, not just a throughput number.
  * just bench-write concurrency sweep shows the plateau move above the current ~84k/384-d.
  * The single-client path is not made slower by the window (no unconditional wait — the window should only ever form when work is already queued).

title: [epic] Scale writes out — the single-writer lease is the remaining ceiling
description:
Reads scale horizontally today: any number of read-only instances serve the same shared store, refreshed from the object-store manifest, with readiness gating on staleness. Writes do not. Exactly one instance holds the fenced writer lease (SPEC §14.6), so write throughput is one process's throughput and always will be under the current model.

That is the right design for where nidus has been — the lease is what makes correctness cheap, and the object store's conditional writes are what make the lease safe. It is also, now that the serving edge is hardened (epic nidus-abx) and the lease protocol is solid (nidus-lp4, nidus-lp4.7), the largest remaining scalability ceiling.

Filing as an epic rather than a task because the options are genuinely different products, not implementations of one thing, and choosing between them is the work.

DESIGN
Sketch of the option space, cheapest first. None of these is decided.

  1. FASTER SINGLE WRITER. Not scale-out at all, but likely the best return per unit of risk, and it should be measured before anything below is built. Batch coalescing across concurrent requests (one fsync per batch of upserts rather than per request), parallel encode, a group-commit window. Keeps every existing invariant untouched.

  2. PARTITIONED WRITERS BY COLLECTION. One lease per collection instead of one per store, so N collections admit N concurrent writers. Fits the data model — collections are already independent namespaces sharing an embedding space — and search already merges across collections. Costs: the manifest/commit counter becomes per-partition, compaction and cross-collection consistency need thought, and a reader's staleness becomes a vector rather than a number. Probably the natural next step if the workload is multi-tenant.

  3. SHARDED WRITERS BY ROW RANGE within a collection. Genuine horizontal write scale, and a different database: routing, rebalancing, a shard map, and scatter-gather search with per-shard top-k merging. Big. Only justified by a workload that partition-by-collection cannot serve.

  4. ACCEPT THE CEILING AND SAY SO. Document single-writer throughput as a positioning boundary and point users at option 1 plus vertical scale. A legitimate answer for a store that positions itself for development and small-scale use.

PREREQUISITE, and the first actual task: MEASURE. benchmarks/ reports ~139-169k ingest/s in-process and ~14k/s over HTTP (nidus-8fn) — a 10x gap that says the bottleneck today is very likely the HTTP/JSON path, not the lease. Scaling writers out before closing that would be optimising the wrong layer. Get a real number for where a single writer actually saturates, and on what, before picking from the list above.

ACCEPTANCE CRITERIA
A measured account of what limits write throughput today, and an explicit decision between options 1-4 recorded here. Not code — the decision is the deliverable.
design:
DECISION: option 1 (faster single writer) + option 4 (document the ceiling).
Do NOT build option 2 (per-collection leases) or option 3 (row-range shards).

nidus does not have a write scale-out problem. It has a per-request efficiency
problem, and a large amount of unclaimed headroom inside one writer.

── HOW IT WAS MEASURED ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────
New bench: `just bench-write` (benchmarks/src/write.rs, nidus-bench-write). It
times each stage a vector passes through on its way in — client JSON encode,
server JSON decode, Nidus::upsert without fsync, the fsync, and the real HTTP
round trip against a live `nidus serve` — then sweeps batch size and concurrent
writers. Whatever the round trip costs beyond the sum of the parts is reported
as a residual (sockets, tokio hop, middleware, RwLock), so nothing hides in it.
Release build, dev machine (macOS/APFS, sync_all = F_FULLFSYNC), n=50k.

── WHERE A VECTOR'S TIME GOES (batch=1000, us/vector) ───────────────────────
                          dim=384      dim=768
  client JSON encode         9.57        18.93   (client-side, off the server)
  server JSON decode         5.53        10.80
  store append (no fsync)    8.25         9.56
  fsync (per batch)          5.18         4.91
  = in-process durable      13.43        14.47
  HTTP round trip           30.10        49.80
  of which transport+rt     11.14        24.53

The store itself is 45% (384-d) / 29% (768-d) of the HTTP cost. The majority is
JSON + transport. Note the store's per-vector cost barely moves with dimension
(13.43 -> 14.47) while JSON roughly doubles (15.1 -> 29.7): the JSON path scales
with dimension, the store path does not.

── FINDING 1: THE LEASE IS NOT THE BOTTLENECK, AND IS NOWHERE NEAR IT ───────
Nothing in the measured write path is lease work. More decisively, one writer
PROCESS is not limited to its single-client rate:

  concurrent writers, vectors/s (batch=1000)
  clients    dim=384        dim=768
    1          33k            20k
    2          64k (1.93x)    39k (1.93x)
    4          82k (2.48x)    70k (3.48x)
    8          84k (2.54x)    67k (3.32x)

Throughput nearly doubles at two clients and plateaus at ~84k / ~67k vec/s. That
plateau sits right on the in-process durable rate (73k / 72k), i.e. the asymptote
is the store's exclusive critical section — and the single-client number was just
pipeline serialisation (encode -> send -> decode -> store -> reply, in series),
not a server limit at all.

So the real single-writer ceiling is ~70-85k vec/s, roughly 2.5-3.5x above what a
naive single-threaded client sees. Options 2 and 3 would add partitioning,
routing, a shard map and scatter-gather merging in order to raise a ceiling that
nobody is currently reaching, while the cheap headroom below it goes unclaimed.
That is precisely the "optimising the wrong layer" this epic's prerequisite was
written to prevent.

── FINDING 2: BATCH SIZE DOMINATES EVERYTHING ELSE ──────────────────────────
  records/request   vectors/s over HTTP (1 client, 384-d)
        1                 125
       10                  1k
      100                  9k
     1000                 33k

A 264x swing on identical code. Per-request fixed cost (one round trip, one
fsync) is ~7.6ms and is paid whether the request carries 1 record or 1000.

── FINDING 3 (BUG, FILED AS nidus-4h2) ──────────────────────────────────────
Half that per-call cost is an unconditional fsync. `upsert` phase 2 syncs `data`
regardless of policy, while phase 4 correctly honours it — so `Fsync::OnFlush`,
sold as "faster, weaker durability", still pays ~3.8ms of disk barrier per call
and delivers about half the speedup it promises. Constant across store sizes.
P1, one-line guard, but it changes crash-recovery behaviour so it gets its own
review and its own recovery test rather than riding along in a bench PR.

── WHAT TO DO, IN RETURN-PER-RISK ORDER ─────────────────────────────────────
1. nidus-4h2 — gate the phase-2 data fsync on PerBatch. One line, ~2x on
   OnFlush small writes, no new concepts.
2. Group commit / batch coalescing (option 1 proper). The concurrency sweep
   shows 2-8 upserts genuinely in flight at once, each paying its own barrier.
   Merging concurrent commits into one fsync is where the ~84k plateau moves,
   and it keeps every existing invariant.
3. Client guidance — DONE in this PR: docs/guides/http-server.md now has a
   "Getting write throughput" section with the batch-size table and the
   concurrency advice. This is option 4's useful half and cost nothing.
4. Binary wire format. Decode is 18% (384-d) / 22% (768-d) of the round trip and
   grows with dimension, so it is real but not dominant. Quantify against
   group commit before building; deferred.

── WHEN TO RE-OPEN SCALE-OUT ────────────────────────────────────────────────
Re-open options 2/3 when either is true, and not before:
  * a single writer sustaining ~70-85k vec/s is demonstrably the constraint on a
    real workload (i.e. after 1 and 2 above have landed and been re-measured), or
  * per-collection leases are wanted for multi-tenant ISOLATION rather than
    throughput — a different justification, and a legitimate one, but it should
    be argued on isolation and not smuggled in as a performance change.

title: A client that withholds its request body pins a concurrency permit
description:
Found while probing an unrelated CI failure on PR #62 (nidus-abx.2), not by design — worth recording because it is a gap the backpressure work itself opened.

The permit is acquired in the backpressure middleware, which runs BEFORE the handler awaits the request body. So a client that sends complete headers with a Content-Length and then withholds the body holds a permit for as long as it stays silent. Classic slow-loris shape, now pointed at admission control rather than at memory.

REPRODUCED, not theorised. With --max-concurrent-requests 1 --read-timeout 0, one raw socket sending only:

    POST /search HTTP/1.1
    Host: ...
    Content-Length: 4096
    <no body>

pins the single permit, and every subsequent request from another connection is shed with 503 indefinitely.

WHETHER THIS IS A REGRESSION: partly. Before nidus-abx.2 there was no concurrency limit, so there were no permits to exhaust — a slow client cost a connection and some memory and nothing else. The limit is a real improvement against the failure mode it targets (unbounded in-flight bodies competing with the in-RAM working set), but it introduced an admission pool that a cheap, low-bandwidth client can now occupy.

WHAT ALREADY BOUNDS IT
  * --read-timeout defaults to 30s and DOES cover this: the timeout wraps next.run(req), which includes the handler awaiting the body. So by default a pinned permit is released after 30s.
  * The default concurrency limit is 8x cores floored at 64, so an attacker needs 64 concurrent silent connections to shed all traffic — cheap, but not free.
  * --read-timeout 0 removes the bound entirely, and the flag is currently documented as 'disables it' with no mention that it also disables this protection.

DESIGN
Smallest honest fix is documentation: say in the server guide that --read-timeout is also the slow-client bound, that setting it to 0 removes that bound, and that slow-client/slowloris protection belongs at the same proxy that terminates TLS and rate-limits (consistent with the division of responsibility already documented for nidus-abx.2/.6).

Beyond that, consider whether a separate, shorter header-to-body deadline is worth it — a body should arrive in far less than the 30s a legitimate large SEARCH may take to compute. That is a different bound from --read-timeout (time to receive the request vs time to serve it), and conflating them is why one number has to cover both today. Do NOT reach for per-IP connection limits here; that is the proxy's job.

Also worth deciding: whether acquiring the permit before the body is read is the right order at all. Acquiring after would make this vanish, but would put unbounded in-flight bodies back above the admission gate — which is the exact thing nidus-abx.2 exists to stop. The current order is probably right and the deadline is the correct lever; that reasoning should be written down either way.
close_reason: Fixed in PR #62 via --body-idle-timeout: an http_body::Body wrapper that abandons a request body which stops delivering frames (default 15s, 0 disables). IDLE not total, so a large slow upload is never cut off. Permit still held during body arrival (deliberate — bounds concurrent buffering), so the pin window is shortened, not eliminated; proxy-level slow-client defence remains the real answer, as documented. e2e test drives it over a raw socket and was verified to FAIL without the fix. http-body added to Cargo.toml but adds zero packages/build time (axum already depends on the same version); absent from the pure library tree.

title: TLS and exposure posture is undocumented (token crosses the network in cleartext)
description:
nidus serve speaks plain HTTP and nothing else. There is no TLS support in the server (no rustls or native-tls anywhere in src/server/), and — the actual problem — the docs never say so.

Searching the deployment guide (docs/src/content/docs/guides/cli-and-server.md) for tls/https/proxy finds only install-script URLs. So a reader following the cluster deployment section, which does document --token, gets an authenticated server and no indication that the credential they just configured crosses the network in cleartext on every request, along with every vector, document ID, and metadata value.

That is the gap worth closing. Not "nidus should terminate TLS" — for this positioning, terminating at an ingress/sidecar/service mesh is very likely the RIGHT architecture, and adding rustls to the default build would pull a TLS stack into the server for a job the surrounding infrastructure already does better. The defect is that the boundary is undocumented, so a user cannot tell whether HTTP-only is a considered decision with a named prerequisite or simply something nobody thought about.

Note the interaction with the shipped Helm chart (charts/nidus/): it exposes a Service and documents --token via values, so it currently makes cleartext-token-over-the-network the easy default path. Whatever stance is chosen has to be reflected there too, not just in prose.

Also worth stating explicitly in the same place: the server binds whatever --addr says, so a careless 0.0.0.0 bind with no token is an unauthenticated, world-readable-and-writable vector store. The startup line already announces the bind address and whether auth is on (src/server/mod.rs:147-158), which is the natural place to escalate.
design:
Documentation first, and it may be the whole fix:

  * A "Securing a deployment" section in the CLI/server guide stating plainly that nidus serves plain HTTP by design and that TLS is expected to be terminated in front of it (ingress, sidecar, or mesh), with a worked example. Say what --token does and does not protect: it authenticates a caller, it does not confer confidentiality.
  * Say where rate limiting belongs (the proxy — see nidus-abx.2, which deliberately does not implement it) so the division of responsibility is explicit rather than implied by omission.
  * Update the chart to match: document the expected ingress/TLS shape in values.yaml rather than leaving the Service as the only story.

Then one small code change, because a doc nobody reads is a weak control. On startup, WARN when the configuration is plausibly unsafe:

  * a token is configured but the bind address is not loopback (the credential will cross a network that may not be encrypted), and
  * no token is configured and the bind address is not loopback (an unauthenticated store reachable off-box).

Warn, do NOT refuse. Refusing would break every legitimate deployment that terminates TLS at a proxy — which is the architecture being recommended — so this must stay advisory. Extend the existing startup line rather than inventing a new mechanism; it already reports the bound address and whether auth is required, so it is the honest place for the caveat.

Explicitly OUT OF SCOPE unless a user asks: terminating TLS in-process. Record the reasoning (the proxy does it better; rustls in the default build is a dependency-budget decision under CLAUDE.md; the sans-IO S3/GCS clients already pull ring for OUTBOUND TLS, which is a different concern from serving it) so a future reader does not have to re-derive it.
acceptance_criteria: The docs and the chart state plainly that nidus serves plain HTTP, that TLS is terminated in front of it, and what --token does and does not protect; the startup line warns on a non-loopback bind with a token (cleartext credential) or without one (unauthenticated store); the warning never refuses to start.
notes:
SHIPPED (2026-07-25). Documentation first, as the issue framed it, plus the small advisory code change.

DOCS — docs/src/content/docs/guides/http-server.md gains a "Securing a deployment" section stating plainly that nidus serves plain HTTP BY DESIGN (TLS terminates at an ingress/sidecar/mesh, which does it better than a TLS stack compiled into a vector store), that --token authenticates a caller and confers NO confidentiality, that the bind address is the real perimeter, and that rate limiting belongs at the proxy (cross-referencing nidus-abx.2, which deliberately does not implement it). Worked nginx example with a loopback upstream. A "What the token model is, and is not" subsection makes the single-static-secret boundary explicit (nidus-abx.5's other half). The HTTP API reference gains 503/504 rows and a "Retrying" section.

CHART — charts/nidus/values.yaml: the auth block now carries the full posture (plain HTTP, ClusterIP is only as private as the CNI, terminate TLS the moment you expose it, rate limiting on the ingress, token model boundaries). The ingress block says outright that an empty `tls:` publishes the token and every vector in cleartext, and points at the two proxy settings that otherwise break nidus (proxy-body-size vs --max-body-bytes, proxy-read-timeout vs --write-timeout). Chart version 0.4.0 -> 0.5.0.

CODE — warn_on_exposure() on the startup path: a non-loopback bind WITH a token warns that the credential crosses the network in cleartext; WITHOUT one, that the store is readable and writable by anyone who can reach it. Warns, never refuses — refusing would break every deployment that terminates TLS at a proxy, which is the recommended architecture. An unknown bind address says nothing rather than guessing: a false security warning is how operators learn to ignore the real one. Loopback is silent, because a warning on every `nidus serve` on a laptop is one people scroll past.

The decision is split from the emission (fn exposure() -> Exposure) so the classification is unit-tested exactly, without a test binding a real off-box socket on whatever machine runs it. The e2e side asserts the complement: a loopback server prints no warning.

OUT OF SCOPE, recorded: terminating TLS in-process. The proxy does it better; rustls in the default build is a dependency-budget decision under CLAUDE.md; and the ring already in the tree is for OUTBOUND TLS in the S3/GCS clients, which is a different concern from serving it.

NOTE for a follow-up (not this PR): charts/nidus/Chart.yaml appVersion is still 0.26.0 while the crate is 0.35.0. Pre-existing drift, and the new values default to "" so nothing is emitted against an older image — but the chart's default image tag is well behind.

title: Observability: traffic-level metrics and correlatable, levelled logs
description:
There is no way to see what an instance is DOING. GET /cluster and GET /stats (added by nidus-lp4.4/.5) report STATE — role, lease owner, commit counter, staleness, footprint — which was the right first step and covers "who is the writer" during an incident. Neither reports TRAFFIC.

Missing, and each is a question an on-call engineer actually asks:

  * Request rate, latency distribution, and error rate, by route. Today the only way to know how the server is performing is to measure from outside it. nidus-8fn measured the HTTP path at ~100-140us of constant overhead in a benchmark, but a running instance exposes nothing comparable.
  * Search-specific cost: vectors scanned per query, whether the ANN path or the brute-force tail served it, quantized-vs-f32 rerank counts. This is the difference between "queries are slow" and "queries are slow BECAUSE the index is not being used".
  * Lease and fencing events as COUNTERS, not just current state: renewals attempted/succeeded/failed, transient-vs-definitive failures (the distinction introduced by nidus-lp4.7), fences latched, takeovers. The epic that just closed showed why: reconstructing a lease incident required reading stderr from two processes and correlating by pid. A counter for "lease renewals that failed transiently" would have shown the object store misbehaving long before anything broke.
  * Memory-tier and object-store health: request counts, retry counts, latency. src/http.rs already implements backoff and a dead-pooled-connection retry (commit 7b36ec9) — those retries are invisible today, so a degrading backend looks like nothing at all until it fails outright.

Logging has the same shape of gap: it is bare eprintln! throughout (for example src/server/mod.rs:158, :175, and the lease lines added by nidus-lp4.7). No levels, so there is no way to turn detail up in production or down in a test; no request IDs, so a slow request cannot be correlated with the lease renewal that overlapped it; no machine-readable structure, so a log aggregator cannot query any of it. NIDUS_LEASE_DEBUG=1 is a deliberately crude on/off for one subsystem and shows what the general mechanism should be.
design:
Prometheus text format on GET /metrics, hand-rolled. No new dependency: the format is a few lines of text, and a HashMap of atomic counters plus a fixed-bucket histogram is well under a hundred lines. This matters — pulling in the prometheus crate (or opentelemetry, far worse) would blow the build-and-ship budget CLAUDE.md protects, and nidus already hand-rolls its CRC32 for exactly this reason.

Decide up front whether /metrics requires the bearer token. Recommend NO (same reasoning as /health and /ready in the auth middleware, src/server/mod.rs:350-351: a scraper that gets a 401 reports the target as down), but note that metrics leak collection names and traffic shape, so it should be documented as "expose on a scrape-only path" alongside the TLS stance in nidus-abx.7.

For logging, prefer levels + structure WITHOUT adding tracing/tracing-subscriber. That pair is popular and would be idiomatic, but it is a real dependency-tree decision, not an implementation detail, so raise it as its own question rather than assuming it. A minimal alternative that fits the existing style: a log! macro with a level filtered by NIDUS_LOG, emitting one key=value line per event, and a request ID generated in middleware and threaded through the handler. That subsumes the ad-hoc NIDUS_LEASE_DEBUG hook rather than sitting beside it.

Cheapness is a hard constraint on the metrics path: recording must be atomic increments only, never a lock, or the observability layer becomes its own contention point on a store that is already lock-serialised. Explicitly do NOT put a metrics mutex anywhere near the store lock.
acceptance_criteria: A scrape endpoint exposes request rate/latency/errors by route, search-path costs, and lease/fencing counters; logs carry levels and a per-request ID and are machine-parseable; the metrics path takes no locks; and no dependency is added without an explicit decision recorded on this issue.
notes:
DECIDED (implementation, 2026-07-25): NO NEW DEPENDENCY, for either half. The issue asked for this to be explicit, so:

* Metrics: hand-rolled Prometheus text. `prometheus` (let alone `opentelemetry`) would blow the build-and-ship budget for a format that is a few lines of writeln!. Same trade as crc.rs. Whole-crate clean build measured 4.2s after this change.
* Logging: NOT tracing/tracing-subscriber. It is the idiomatic answer and would be fine for a bigger service, but it is a dependency-tree decision, and it would land in the LIBRARY tree — every `cargo add nidus` consumer would pay for it. What the crate needs is levels, key=value structure, and a request id; src/diag.rs is ~120 lines of that. The shape is one a tracing migration would keep if ever wanted.

SHIPPED
- src/metrics.rs (library, always compiled): lock-free process-wide counters. Lease (attempts/ok/transient/lost/fenced/wait-errors — the transient-vs-definitive split from nidus-lp4.7 is now a counter, which is the thing that would have shown the object store misbehaving before anything broke), backend retries, refresh failures, search path (queries + which path served them: ann / segmented / quantized / exact, plus vectors_scanned and reranked). `counters()` DESTRUCTURES Metrics, so adding a counter without exporting it is a compile error.
- src/server/metrics.rs (cli): per-route request counts by status class, latency histogram (15 buckets, 0.5ms..60s — the honest range spans five orders of magnitude), shed/timed-out/cancelled counters, in-flight gauge, plus nidus_ready / nidus_writer_fenced / nidus_staleness_seconds.
- src/diag.rs: `diag!(Level, target, msg, k => v, ...)` -> logfmt on stderr, level from NIDUS_LOG (error|warn|info|debug|trace|off, default info). Level check happens before argument evaluation. NIDUS_LEASE_DEBUG now simply means debug — the crude one-subsystem hook is subsumed, not sitting beside the general one. Every eprintln! diagnostic in the crate converted.
- Request ids: honoured from inbound X-Request-Id (validated — length-capped and charset-filtered, because an unvalidated header value in a log line is a log-injection primitive), minted otherwise, echoed on the response, present on every access line.

CARDINALITY / DISCLOSURE. Route labels are TEMPLATES and route_index() returns an index into a compile-time ROUTES array, so a collection name physically cannot reach a label. That bounds cardinality (an unbounded label set is the classic way to take a Prometheus server down) and it is what makes /metrics unauthenticated defensible: the scrape exposes traffic shape, never data. Decision on auth: NO token, same reasoning as /health and /ready — a scraper that gets a 401 reports the target as down. Documented as a scrape-only path alongside the TLS stance (nidus-abx.6).

CHEAPNESS. Recording is fetch_add(Relaxed) on a fixed preallocated array — no map, no allocation, no lock anywhere near the store lock. The /metrics handler takes no store lock either, so a scrape during a multi-minute upsert answers instantly.

TWO BUGS CAUGHT IN SELF-REVIEW, both fixed:
- The in-flight gauge was an inc()/dec() pair around the await. axum drops the handler future on client disconnect, so dec() would never run and the gauge would ratchet upward forever — a metric that becomes a lie on exactly the traffic pattern it is watched for. Now an RAII guard, which also gave us nidus_http_requests_cancelled_total for free.
- nidus_ready was re-deriving readiness and had already drifted from GET /ready (it omitted the staleness bound), so a reader that stopped refreshing would show ready=1 on the dashboard while /ready 503'd it out of the load balancer. Factored into one readiness_check(), with a test asserting the gauge and the probe agree.

title: Lease observability: who holds it, until when, and did we lose it
description:
There is currently no way to inspect cluster lease state from outside the process. On-call cannot answer: which instance holds the writer lease, when does it expire, has this instance been fenced, how many times has the lease changed hands?

The lease object already carries an owner token and a timestamp (src/backend/object.rs lock_body(ts, owner)), so the data exists — it is simply not surfaced.

Shape: extend /stats (or a /cluster endpoint) with the instance's role (writer / standby / reader), whether it currently believes it holds the lease, the lease's owner token and expiry, and the last observed commit counter. Enough for a dashboard and an alert on 'no instance holds the writer lease for > N seconds'.

Pair with structured logging of lease transitions (acquired / renewed / lost / reclaimed) — a fenced writer currently surfaces only as a request-level 'writer lease lost' error, so a takeover leaves no clear trace in the logs to correlate an incident against.

Keep it cheap: serve from cached state, no object-store round trip per request (same constraint as nidus-lp4.1).
notes: IMPLEMENTED on branch cluster-hardening (v0.32.0, chart 0.4.0). See the commit for detail; verified by new e2e tests against real minio+valkey.
close_reason: Shipped in PR #58 (v0.32.0): GET /cluster reports role, holds_writer_handle, fenced, lease_owner, commit_version, staleness_secs. Verified by e2e cluster_endpoint_distinguishes_writer_from_reader.

title: Reader staleness: expose it, and bound it
description:
A cluster reader adopts state at open and only advances when something calls POST /refresh (added in nidus-6bb). Correct and cheap, but for production there is no way to answer 'how stale is this reader?' — the question every incident starts with.

Missing:
1. An exposed staleness measure — e.g. /stats reporting the manifest version/commit counter the reader is serving, and how far behind the store's current one it is. Today the only way to know is to compare doc counts by hand.
2. An optional bound: a reader that has not successfully refreshed within N seconds should report NOT READY (composes with nidus-lp4.1) so a load balancer stops sending it reads, rather than silently serving old results forever.
3. Optional self-refresh on an interval, so a deployment does not need a sidecar or cron just to stay current. Explicitly a bounded-cost opt-in — the reason /refresh is manual is that refreshing per read puts a manifest GET on the hot path of exactly the read-heavy fan-out this mode exists for (measured in nidus-8fn: HTTP query overhead is ~100-140us constant, and a manifest fetch would dwarf it).

Item 3 was deliberately NOT done in nidus-6bb — the user chose the explicit endpoint over auto-refresh-on-read. An interval refresher is a different thing from per-read refresh and does not contradict that choice.
notes: IMPLEMENTED on branch cluster-hardening (v0.32.0, chart 0.4.0). See the commit for detail; verified by new e2e tests against real minio+valkey.

title: Benchmark the HTTP server path in release mode (server overhead vs in-process)
description:
Remaining gap after nidus-1e6.5. Every cell in benchmarks/ drives Nidus IN-PROCESS (build_store -> Nidus::open_in_memory / a local store), so nidus serve's own cost is not benchmarked anywhere in release mode:
  - JSON encode/decode of a 384/768-float vector per request (likely the dominant server-side cost, and entirely unmeasured)
  - the Arc<RwLock<Nidus>> + spawn_blocking hop
  - socket framing / connection handling, and behaviour under concurrent clients

tests/e2e/scale.rs now asserts CORRECTNESS at 10k x 384-d over HTTP and prints timings, but it is a DEBUG build with order-of-magnitude ceilings by design — it cannot answer 'what does the server cost us' or catch a 30% regression.

Shape: add an HTTP engine adapter to nidus-bench alongside the existing nidus/duckdb/lancedb ones, so the SAME harness and dataset compare in-process vs over-HTTP and the parity table gains a 'nidus (server)' row. Reuse the existing data/metrics/report modules — do NOT fork the harness (always-dedupe-code). Report only; do not gate PRs on it (see the flake reasoning in nidus-1e6.5).

Worth doing before anyone advertises server throughput numbers, and it would quantify whether a binary/msgpack wire format is worth considering.
close_reason:
Implemented on branch e2e-server-harness (v0.30.0, PR #56). New 'server' engine adapter (benchmarks/src/engines/server.rs, behind the opt-in 'server' feature) spawns nidus serve and drives the SAME dataset over HTTP, so the parity table shows a 'nidus (server)' row directly beneath 'nidus'. New just bench-server builds the release binary first and passes NIDUS_BIN (benchmarking a debug binary measures nothing).

MEASURED (release, dev machine):
  n=10k  dim=384  — nidus 305us p50 / 139k ingest/s | server 440us p50 / 14k/s
  n=100k dim=768  — nidus 5.82ms p50 / 169k ingest/s | server 5.90ms p50 / 14k/s

FINDING: HTTP query overhead is roughly CONSTANT at ~100-140us per request, not proportional — +44% when the scan is only 305us, but +1.4% once it is milliseconds. So the server is essentially free for real-sized corpora and only visible on tiny ones. INGEST is the real cost: ~14k vec/s over HTTP vs 139-169k in-process, a 10-12x penalty that DOES scale with volume, i.e. JSON float encoding dominates. Recall stays 100.0% both ways, so the HTTP path does not distort results. Anyone quoting nidus throughput must quote the row matching how they run it; this also quantifies what a binary wire format could buy on ingest.

Not shared with tests/e2e/harness.rs deliberately: different crate (unreachable), and the harness panics with child stderr attached, which is right for an assertion and wrong for a benchmark that must return Result.

title: Docs sidebar active link flickers/lags during view-transition navigation
description: The custom docs Sidebar (position:fixed) was captured in Astro ClientRouter's full-page ::view-transition-old/new(root) crossfade. title: Segment-based storage: the scale model (SPEC §14)
description:
Rearchitect the storage layer so scaling is a quantity of one architecture, not a separate mode: durable objects on the persistence backend are the source of truth, a running process is a cache over them, and the single in-RAM data matrix + one log become immutable SEGMENTS + a WAL + a manifest. Fully designed in SPEC §14 (PR #32). Brute-force stays the exact default for the small/recent tail; IVF indexes the cold bulk (per-segment, size-driven). No public API change (§4).

## Context
Grew out of the cluster-mode discussion: cluster mode should be a CONSEQUENCE of this model (shared backend + versioned manifest + race-free writer lease from nidus-a7c), requiring shared persistence + shared memory tier; local FS/RAM are single-node by definition.
design: See SPEC §14. Principle (§14.1): object store is truth, compute caches it. Segments (§14.2) are the unit of >RAM / incremental cloud writes / distribution / maintainable per-segment indexing / background-merge compaction. Brute-force is the tail not the engine (§14.3); IVF over HNSW for the object-backed path. Log-first async indexing (§14.4). Non-negotiables (§14.5): exact/zero-config local, forbid(unsafe), <1min build, §4 API unchanged. Phasing front-loads single-node payoff (§14.6).
close_reason: All 5 phases shipped (0.18.0–0.22.0): segment format + manifest + WAL→segment seal (vuq.1), per-segment IVF + exhaustive tail (vuq.2), per-segment mmap (vuq.3), manifest-versioned reader refresh (vuq.4), cooperating-instances cluster mode (vuq.5). The monolith is gone: a store is immutable segments + a WAL + a versioned manifest; scale is a quantity of one architecture (local FS → object store → cooperating instances) via config, not a separate mode. Exact-by-default and the §4 public API held throughout. Follow-ups tracked in nidus-bdg (refresh) and nidus-ahw (cluster hardening).

title: DECISION: zero-FFI vs C-TLS for cloud storage backends (SPEC §13.6)
description: Cloud backends (S3/GCS) need HTTPS → a TLS stack. Verified dep trees: rustls defaults to aws-lc-sys (C); ring provider compiles C+asm; reqwest's rustls path pulls ring; google-cloud-storage pulls ring AND OpenSSL. A pure path exists (rustls + rustls-rustcrypto + hand-built hyper/tokio-rustls = no C) but rustls-rustcrypto is UNAUDITED. S3 auth (Sigv4) is pure HMAC (rusty-s3 clean); GCS auth (tame-oauth) pulls ring for RSA-JWT and would need RustCrypto rsa instead.
acceptance_criteria: Pick (A) Pragmatic: allow audited C TLS (aws-lc/ring) gated behind a non-default feature like cli, so cargo add nidus stays pure — OR (B) Purist: hold zero-FFI via rustls-rustcrypto + hand-rolled auth (bespoke, unaudited crypto). Redis over plain TCP (redis://) needs no TLS and is unaffected; only rediss:// reuses this. Blocks the S3/GCS phase.
notes:
RESOLVED → (A) pragmatic, NOT purist. C/FFI allowed but ONLY behind a non-default 'cloud' feature AND only via crates that don't compile a large C tree. Hard rule: cloud-feature clean build < 1 minute. FORBIDDEN (slow C compile): rustls default aws-lc-sys, vendored OpenSSL, reqwest+tokio+hyper. ALLOWED (fast): sans-IO rusty-s3/tame-gcs + lightweight blocking HTTP (ureq) + TLS via ring or system-linked native-tls. MEASURED: clean debug build of rusty-s3+tame-gcs+ureq (ring included) = ~6s, ~10x under budget. (B) purist rejected: unaudited crypto on a credentialed path is a worse trade than a fast, feature-gated, audited C dep. See SPEC §13.6.
SUPERSEDED detail: NOT feature-gated. All backends compile into the DEFAULT build (no per-backend / no 'cloud' feature). Rationale: a user who outgrows local FS and needs S3 must switch with a one-line runtime change (file:// -> s3://), never a Cargo.toml-edit-and-recompile event. Accepted cost: ring enters the default tree (C toolchain required for all consumers; Miri now covers only our logic, network TLS tests join the miri-ignore set). Measured: full core + all four backends (sync Redis, no tokio/aws-lc/OpenSSL) clean build = ~7.5s. See SPEC §1 + §13.6.
close_reason: Closed

title: Pluggable storage & memory backends: persistence (local/S3/GCS) + shared memory tier (local RAM/Redis/Valkey/Memcached)
description: Generalize the SPEC §5 local directory into a pluggable storage layer: one object-granular, sync `Backend` trait with impls for local files, S3, GCS, and Redis/Valkey, selected by URL scheme (file://, s3://, gs://, redis://). Fully designed in SPEC §13. The on-disk object set (data/log source-of-truth + ann/fts derived caches) is unchanged — only where the bytes live. Search stays backend-independent (never in the query hot path); network backends trade cheaper near-incremental writes for a costlier open (rebuild caches from the download). Both live-backing and snapshot/backup modes are in scope.
design: See SPEC.md §13. Two object classes: source-of-truth (data, log; append-shaped, must be durable) vs derived cache (ann, fts; reconstructable, droppable). Trait is sync by design (§13.2): search is CPU-over-RAM, every backend can be sync (sans-IO S3/GCS + blocking HTTP; redis-rs blocking mode), and a sync trait is dyn-safe for true plug-and-play. Async-only clients quarantine block_on internally.
notes: RESHAPE: this is TWO orthogonal axes, not one storage trait. (1) PERSISTENCE backend = durable source-of-truth bytes (data/log): local files / S3 / GCS. (2) MEMORY TIER = where the in-RAM working set is held for serving: local process RAM (default) / Redis / Valkey / Memcached. Redis/Valkey/Memcached are NOT storage — they are a SHARED, rebuildable cache of the working set (model (a)): loaded into local RAM to serve, never searched over the wire, never authoritative, never larger-than-RAM. The two axes compose. See SPEC §13 (rewritten).

# ANN / HNSW approximate index — opt-in, brute-force stays the default

## Summary
A pure-Rust approximate-nearest-neighbour index (HNSW, or IVF) built over the same
`data` rows. When enabled, `search()` consults the index instead of the full scan.
**Exact brute-force remains the default and is never silently replaced** — ANN is opt-in
via `Config` only. Needed only past brute-force's comfort zone (≫ a few million vectors).

## Positioning decision (not just engineering)
This shifts nidus from "exact" to "**exact by default, approximate opt-in**." That is a
deliberate identity change — keep the default exact, make the opt-in explicit and named,
and document the recall/speed trade honestly. Do not let ANN leak into the default path.

## Constraints (non-negotiable, same as the rest of nidus)
- Pure Rust, **no `*-sys`, no FFI**; `#![forbid(unsafe_code)]` in our code; Miri-clean.
- Additive over the existing on-disk format — the index is an in-RAM structure
  rebuildable from `data` (persistence is a later sub-seam, not v1).

## Config surface (sketch)
- `Config::index(IndexKind::Hnsw { m, ef_construction, .. })`, default `IndexKind::None`
  (brute force). Per-query `ef`/recall knob in `SearchOpts`.

## Design notes (high-level — this is a future epic, own branch)
- Incremental graph build on `upsert`; handle deletes/overwrites (tombstones + periodic
  rebuild on `compact`).
- Composes with quantization: HNSW over int8/binary codes is a common, effective combo
  (cheap distance in the graph walk, f32 rerank at the end).
- Benchmark the brute-force↔ANN crossover point to document *when* to enable it.

## Sequencing
After the binary-quant + scan-cache work lands (this is the follow-on epic). Large enough
to warrant its own branch and incremental PRs.

design:
# Binary quantization first-pass + shared scan-order cache

## Motivation
The f32 first pass is **bandwidth-bound** — the documented ceiling on parallel-scan
gains. int8 cut first-pass memory traffic 4×; binary cuts it **32×** (8× smaller than
int8), so the first pass scales far better with `query_threads`. The kernel is
`u64::count_ones()` (POPCNT) — a single instruction, autovectorizes, **pure safe Rust**,
so it stays **Miri-clean and zero-FFI**. No new dependencies; `just deps` stays empty.

## Soundness / scope — COSINE ONLY
Sign-bit codes approximate **angular (cosine)** similarity (SimHash): for unit vectors,
the Hamming distance between sign vectors is monotone with the angle. It **discards
magnitude**, so it is NOT a sound ranking proxy for `DotProduct` (magnitude matters) or
`Euclidean` (L2). Therefore binary quantization is supported for `Distance::Cosine`
**only** — reject at `open()` with a clear error for the other metrics (suggest int8).
The f32 rerank still yields exact cosine scores for the selected candidate set; binary
only governs candidate *selection*, exactly like the int8 first pass.

## Config surface
Generalize `Quantization` to carry the scheme:
```rust
pub enum QuantKind { Int8, Binary }
pub struct Quantization { pub kind: QuantKind, pub rescore: usize }
impl Quantization {
    pub fn int8()   -> Self { Self { kind: QuantKind::Int8,   rescore: 4  } } // == current Default
    pub fn binary() -> Self { Self { kind: QuantKind::Binary, rescore: 16 } } // coarser → higher overscan
    pub fn rescore(mut self, n: usize) -> Self { self.rescore = n; self }
}
impl Default for Quantization { fn default() -> Self { Self::int8() } }
```
- Small breaking change to the struct literal; acceptable pre-1.0 (0.10.x). Update call
  sites + docs (`config.rs` doc, getting-started, README if shown).
- `Config::quantization: Option<Quantization>` is unchanged in shape; **brute-force f32
  remains the default** (`None`).
- Binary's default `rescore` is higher (16) because the proxy is coarser; final value is
  a tuning knob to settle by benchmark.

## Storage (in-RAM only — NO on-disk format change)
- `BinState { words: Vec<u64>, words_per_row: usize }`, `words_per_row = dim.div_ceil(64)`.
  Memory = `N * words_per_row * 8` ≈ `N*dim/8` bytes.
- Derived from the f32 `data` rows: bit `i` set iff component `i >= 0.0` (treat ±0.0 as
  `>= 0`). Tail bits past `dim` in the last word are zero in both stored rows and query,
  so they never affect the XOR.
- **Scale-free**: unlike int8 there is no `QuantParams`/global scale and no
  `REFIT_GROWTH`. A row's code depends only on its own signs → incremental `upsert` is
  trivially O(batch), append-only, and never needs a refit.
- Refactor the store's quant slot to hold either scheme:
  `enum Quant { Int8(Int8State), Binary(BinState) }`, `quant: Option<Quant>`.

## Kernels (`search/mod.rs`)
- `fn hamming(a: &[u64], b: &[u64]) -> u32` — XOR + `count_ones`, chunked/lane-folded for
  ILP like `dot()`; pure integer ⇒ Miri-clean.
- First-pass score = `-(hamming as f32)` so higher = better (fits the existing `TopK`
  max-semantics) and is monotone with cosine rank for unit vectors.
- `pack_query(q: &[f32]) -> Vec<u64>` using the same sign rule on the normalized query.

## Two-pass wiring (`store/mod.rs`)
- Mirror `search_quantized`: a `score_chunk_bin` analogous to `score_chunk_i8`, fed
  through the existing generic `parallel_topk` (already generic over `T`/`score_one`)
  when `workers > 1`, else serial. Overscan `top_k * rescore` candidates carrying
  `(row, col, id)`.
- f32 rerank of candidates with the real `score_fn`; `min_score` enforced on the f32
  score only (Hamming is an ordering proxy) — identical contract to int8.

## Scan-order cache — folds in nidus-dxt (option 3)
`search()`/`list()` rebuild `scan: Vec<(row, col, id)>` and `sort_unstable_by_key(row)`
on EVERY query (~29% of a 100k/dim768 serial query). The doc set only changes on write.
- Maintain a **cached row-sorted scan index**, updated on the `&mut self` write paths
  (`upsert`/`delete`/`delete_where`/`drop_collection`/`compact`) and read by the `&self`
  search/list paths with no per-query sort.
- **Key insight:** `data.append` returns monotonically increasing rows, so a brand-new
  id always appends to the END of the row order → O(1) maintenance for the common
  indexing path. Overwrites (old row → dead) and deletes remove an entry; flag those and
  do a lazy full rebuild on next read (dxt's recommended low-risk option (a)).
- **Sync constraint:** store runs under `Arc<RwLock>`/`Mutex`, so no `RefCell`. Prefer
  rebuild-eager-on-write (cache is a plain field; appends keep it sorted incrementally;
  deletes/overwrites set a dirty flag → rebuilt on next read) so `search()` stays
  lock-free. Falls back cleanly to current behavior under write-heavy churn.
- Composes with the parallel path: workers take pre-sorted contiguous slices and skip the
  per-chunk sort entirely (dxt noted this).
- MUST stay correct under multi-collection scope, filters (filter after taking sorted
  order — order preserved), dead rows (append-only overwrite), and Miri-clean.

## Testing
- Pure-logic (Miri-clean): `hamming` vs naive across lengths incl. tail bits; sign-pack
  round trip; binary first-pass recall vs exact on synthetic clustered data
  (`recall@k ≥ threshold` for a given `rescore`).
- Reject `Binary` + non-Cosine at `open()`.
- Scan cache: equivalence — same query yields identical ranked ids/scores with cache
  on vs off; correctness under overwrite/delete/multi-collection/filter.
- Bench (`just bench-crit`): new group comparing binary vs int8 vs f32 (latency +
  recall) at dim 384/768, n=100k/1M; sweep `rescore`. Compare scan-cache against the
  `nidus-33k-final` baseline — only keep the cache if it beats current numbers without
  complicating the write path.

## Done =
- Opt-in; default behavior unchanged (brute-force f32).
- `just ci-cli` green, `just miri` green, `just deps` still empty (no new crates).
- Move binary quant in `SPEC.md` §9 from "still deferred" → "shipped"; update the
  CLAUDE.md deferred-seam list; bump docs/README version snippet if a release goes out.

Binary first-pass recall@k meets threshold at the chosen rescore; bench shows it beats int8 on latency for cosine. Binary+non-cosine rejected at open. Scan-cache: identical ranked results cache on/off, correct under overwrite/delete/multi-collection/filter. On ship: move binary quant SPEC §9 deferred->shipped + update CLAUDE.md.

title: Improve parallel-scan scaling (parallelize quant path; cut serial overhead)
description:
Opt-in parallel scan (Config::query_threads) currently gives only ~1.2-1.6x at 4-8 threads. The f32 path is memory-bandwidth-bound (streams the whole matrix), so it's near its physical ceiling there. The real levers:

1. Parallelize the QUANTIZED first-pass. It's the biggest opportunity: int8 moves 4x fewer bytes, so it's compute- not bandwidth-bound and should scale with threads far better than f32. search_quantized() is currently single-threaded regardless of query_threads -- wire the same std::thread::scope chunk+merge pattern (already used for the f32 path in score_chunk/search) into the int8 first pass, then keep the f32 rerank serial (it's only top_k*rescore rows).

2. Cut serial overhead (Amdahl). The scan buffer build + sort_unstable_by_key runs single-threaded before the parallel region and caps speedup. Options: build per-thread scan buffers, or skip the global row-sort on the parallel path (the per-chunk heaps don't need a globally sorted scan -- the storage-order prefetch benefit is per-chunk).

3. Make PARALLEL_SCAN_FLOOR dim-aware. Per-row cost scales with dim, so a fixed 4096-row floor is too coarse; threshold on rows*dim (work) instead of rows.

Validate each with 'just bench-crit parallel_search' (extend it to also sweep the quantized path). Keep it pure-safe-Rust, no new deps, opt-in. Set honest expectations: f32 won't scale linearly; the quant path is where threads should pay off.
design: Reuse score_chunk + the thread::scope merge already in store::search for the int8 path. Don't add a persistent thread pool (spawn cost is microseconds vs millisecond scans -- not the bottleneck).

title: nidus dot() is a scalar reduction — ~1.6x slower than LanceDB SIMD at scale
description: Finding from nidus-bench (epic nidus-rq9): on exact brute-force cosine KNN, nidus is a reproducible ~1.6x slower than LanceDB at 50k-100k x 384 (nidus ~22ms vs lancedb ~13.5ms p50 @100k; stable across runs, all recall 100%). Diagnosis: NOT variance, NOT parallelism (capping RAYON_NUM_THREADS=1/TOKIO_WORKER_THREADS=1 left lancedb unchanged). Root cause: src/search/mod.rs dot() is a sequential f32 reduction (a.iter().zip(b).map(|(x,y)|x*y).sum()) which LLVM can't auto-vectorize without fast-math (FP non-associativity), so it runs scalar. LanceDB's lance-linalg uses explicit SIMD (NEON). nidus sits mid-pack: faster than DuckDB (~30ms), ~1.6x slower than LanceDB. Proposed fix (stays pure safe stable Rust, no unsafe/fast-math/deps): rewrite dot as a chunked reduction with N independent accumulators (e.g. 8 lanes) so each lane is an independent sum LLVM CAN vectorize, combined at the end. Caveat: changes summation order -> slightly different f32 rounding (may reorder exact-tie boundaries; benchmark recall tolerant). Verify with just bench all + just bench-crit before/after.
notes:
FIXED — outcome far exceeded the 1.6x parity goal: nidus is now the FASTEST engine in every benchmark cell (2-6x faster than LanceDB, 4-12x faster than DuckDB), recall 100%.

Three stacked fixes (all pure safe stable Rust, no unsafe/fast-math/deps):
1. SIMD-friendly dot (src/search/mod.rs): 8 independent accumulator lanes (chunks_exact(8) + pairwise fold + scalar tail) so each lane is its own associative reduction LLVM can auto-vectorize. Closed most of the kernel gap (dim=768 reached parity).
2. No-alloc scan (src/store/mod.rs search()): TopK now carries borrowed (&str,&str) during the scan instead of eagerly building (col.to_string(), id.clone()) per row — eliminated ~50M throwaway String allocs at 100k×384. Strings/attrs materialized only for the <=k survivors.
3. Row-sorted sequential scan (src/store/mod.rs search()): collect in-scope filter-passing rows as cheap borrowed tuples, sort_unstable_by_key(row), then walk the data matrix in storage order. The 159MB matrix dwarfs L3, so the old HashMap-iteration order was DRAM-miss-bound at every row boundary; sequential order lets the prefetcher stream it. THIS was the dominant win — criterion search/100k×768 -69.8%.

Numbers (p50, 100k vectors): 384/k10 nidus 5.44ms vs lance 12.29 vs duck 32.29; 768/k10 nidus 8.09 vs lance 24.78 vs duck 69.54; 768/k100 nidus 8.57 vs lance 53.16 vs duck 64.99.

Future (separate issue, NOT done here): the row-sorted scan allocates+sorts an n-element Vec per query; doc set is static between writes, so the sorted order could be cached and invalidated on upsert/delete. Deferred to keep this change focused.

title: In-flight accounting understates work after a deadline fires
description:
`nidus_http_admitted_in_flight` reports fewer requests than are actually running during the tail of an abandoned request.

The concurrency permit is released the moment a deadline fires, because holding it would be worse: the server would shed live traffic on behalf of work nobody is waiting for. But the blocking task keeps running until it notices cancellation, so for that window the gauge is low.

MUCH SMALLER THAN IT WAS. Cooperative cancellation (added alongside nidus-6c2 in PR #62) means the scan now stops within a few thousand rows of the deadline rather than running to completion, so the discrepancy is milliseconds rather than a full scan. This is filed as the residual, not the original problem.

Note the counter is honest about what it names — permits held — and the permit really is released. The question is whether 'admitted in flight' is the useful thing to report, or whether an operator wants 'work actually executing'.

DESIGN
Options, roughly in order of cost:
  * Leave it and document the semantics precisely on the metric's HELP text. Probably right: the window is now small and the alternative readings each have their own lie.
  * A second gauge, nidus_http_orphaned_in_flight, incremented when a deadline fires and decremented when the blocking task finally returns. Needs the task to signal completion back to something that outlives the dropped response future — an Arc holding a Drop guard threaded into the spawn_blocking closure would do it.
  * Fold it into the existing gauge so it reports permits + orphans. Rejected on sight: the gauge would then no longer correspond to the admission decision it is named after, which is the thing an operator correlates with shed counts.

Measure before building: nidus_http_requests_timed_out_total already says how often this window is even entered. If it is ~0 in practice, this is not worth a second gauge.
close_reason:
Resolved as "leave the gauge, document the semantics precisely" — the first option in the issue, which it already called probably right.

The measurement the issue asked for is available at zero cost: nidus_http_requests_timed_out_total counts exactly how many times the discrepancy window is entered, and cooperative cancellation (PR #62) bounded that window to milliseconds. A second gauge would buy a more precise answer to a question the existing counter already answers well enough to act on, at the cost of threading a Drop guard through spawn_blocking so it outlives the dropped response future.

SHIPPED
  * src/server/metrics.rs — the admitted gauge HELP now reads "Concurrency permits held: store-touching requests admitted and not yet released, excluding work whose deadline already fired", so the exclusion is delivered to whoever reads the scrape rather than living only in an issue. timed_out HELP now says clients freed AND the scan signalled to stop. requests_in_flight now says probes are included.
  * A module-doc section explaining the two gauges, why the permit gauge is named after the admission decision, and why folding orphans into it was rejected (it would stop corresponding to the shed count, which is the only reason to graph it).
  * A test — the_two_in_flight_gauges_are_distinct_and_self_describing — asserting both gauges carry HELP/TYPE and that the permit gauge names both what it counts and what it excludes. The drift this guards against is invisible in a scrape, so it needed pinning.
  * docs/guides/http-server.md — a "The two in-flight gauges" table plus the deadline caveat.
  * Fixed a STALE doc found next door: --read-timeout claimed "a scan runs to completion regardless — cancelling it would need a cooperative check in the scan loop, which nidus does not have". nidus has had exactly that since PR #62. Same honesty problem this issue is about, one layer up.

Re-open if nidus_http_requests_timed_out_total ever climbs on a real deployment; that is the trigger the issue itself named for building the orphan gauge.

title: [BUG] Bearer token is compared in non-constant time (timing side channel)
description:
The bearer token is compared with a plain string inequality (src/server/mod.rs:358):

    if presented != Some(expected.as_ref()) {

str equality short-circuits on the first differing byte, so comparison time varies with how many leading bytes match. That is a textbook timing side channel on a secret.

Honest severity assessment: LOW, and it should be filed as low rather than dressed up. Exploiting a remote timing oracle across a network, against a comparison of a handful of bytes, requires an enormous number of samples to lift the jitter floor, and an attacker who can do that against a token of any real entropy has easier options. It is on this list because it is (a) unambiguously the wrong primitive for a secret, (b) the first thing any security review or auditor flags, and (c) roughly a ten-line fix, so the cost/benefit is trivially favourable.

Related, and arguably more consequential than the timing itself: there is ONE static token with no rotation story, no scoping (any valid token can read every collection, write, compact, and hit /refresh), and no way to revoke one instance's credential without restarting every instance. That may well be the right scope for nidus's positioning, but it is currently undocumented, so a user cannot tell whether it is a considered boundary or an oversight. Decide and write it down.
design:
Constant-time comparison without a new dependency: fold a XOR of every byte pair into an accumulator and compare once at the end, so the work does not depend on where the first mismatch is. The subtle crate is the usual answer and is tiny, but this is small enough to keep dependency-free in the spirit of crc.rs.

Handle the length case deliberately: comparing different-length inputs leaks the length regardless, so compare lengths first and then run the fixed-time loop over the expected token. Leaking the token LENGTH is acceptable; leaking a prefix match is not.

Put it in one place. The auth middleware is the only consumer today, but a helper (or a small ConstantTimeToken newtype wrapping the String, with equality implemented once) prevents a future second call site from reintroducing the plain comparison — the always-dedupe-code rule applies.

Test it for CORRECTNESS, not for timing. A timing assertion would flake on any shared runner and prove nothing; assert instead that valid tokens are accepted, invalid ones rejected, and that a token which is a strict prefix of the expected value is rejected.

Separately, document the token model explicitly (single shared secret, no rotation, no per-collection scoping, all-or-nothing access) so the boundary is a stated design choice. That documentation belongs with nidus-abx.7, which owns the surrounding TLS posture; land the two together.
acceptance_criteria: Token comparison runs in time independent of how many leading bytes match, implemented in exactly one place, with tests covering valid, invalid, and prefix-of-valid tokens. The token model's boundaries (single static secret, no rotation, no scoping) are documented as a deliberate choice.
notes:
FIXED (2026-07-25) in src/server/auth.rs. Token is now a newtype over Arc<str> with a `verify` that compares in constant time: length checked first (leaking the LENGTH is acceptable and unavoidable; leaking a PREFIX MATCH is not), then a XOR fold over every byte pair into one accumulator, tested once at the end, with std::hint::black_box so a future optimiser cannot abandon the fold early. No dependency — `subtle` is tiny but so is this, and crc.rs sets the precedent.

The newtype is the point, not just the loop: Token has no accessor that hands the bytes back, so a future second call site cannot reintroduce `presented == expected`. The plain comparison is unreachable, not merely discouraged.

Tests are for CORRECTNESS, not timing (a timing assertion flakes on any shared runner and proves nothing): valid accepted; same-length-different-bytes rejected; every strict prefix rejected (the case a broken constant-time comparison gets wrong — folding over min(len) would accept it); superstring rejected; non-ASCII byte-exact, with one case that reaches the fold and one caught by the length check.

TOKEN MODEL documented as a deliberate boundary, in both the server guide ("What the token model is, and is not") and charts/nidus/values.yaml: one static shared secret, no rotation without a restart, no per-collection or read-only scoping, no user identity. Landed together with nidus-abx.6 as one coherent security-posture change, as the issue asked.
close_reason: Closed

title: Lease renewal is op-driven only: a slow-but-alive writer can be fenced mid-batch
description:
The writer lease is renewed at the START of each write batch — op-driven, deliberately no background thread (SPEC §14.6, and 'no background threads' is a stated design property). CAS then refuses any write from a writer superseded mid-batch, which is SAFE: the e2e SIGSTOP test confirms committed data is never clobbered.

The availability cost, though: a writer that is ALIVE but slow — a very large batch, a stalled object-store PUT, a long GC pause — can exceed lock_ttl mid-batch, get fenced, and have to be restarted, even though nothing was actually wrong with it. Safety is preserved; availability is not. Under production load that is a self-inflicted outage whose likelihood rises with batch size.

Options, none obviously right:
(a) Renew mid-batch at object-write boundaries rather than only at batch start — keeps the no-background-thread property, but adds a lease write per object.
(b) An opt-in background renewal thread — simplest and most robust, but breaks a stated design property, so it needs to be an explicit, documented opt-in.
(c) Document a lock_ttl sizing rule against the largest expected batch, and expose enough telemetry (nidus-lp4.5) to see near-misses. Cheapest; leaves the failure mode in place.

Prerequisite for judging this: measure how close real batches come to a default TTL. nidus-8fn showed HTTP ingest at ~14k vec/s, so a 1M-vector batch is ~70s — well past a 60s default lock_ttl, which suggests this is NOT theoretical.
notes:
PARTIAL on branch cluster-hardening (v0.32.0). Added a Drop-free LeaseRenewer + a server-side renewal timer at lock_ttl/3, independent of the store lock so it survives a long write holding the guard. Chose the server-timer approach over the issue's option (a) (renew at object-write boundaries) because a SINGLE object PUT can itself exceed the TTL, and over option (b) (library background thread) because 'no background threads' is a stated property of the sync core — the server is already async, so the timer lives there.

FOUND AND FIXED en route: ClusterLease had Clone added so a renewer could hold a handle, but it is an OWNING guard whose Drop deletes the lease object, so every cloned handle released the lease when dropped. Hence LeaseRenewer (key + owner, no Drop).

NOT CLOSED: the idle-writer reproduction still fails — see nidus-lp4.6b (P0, split-brain). Until that is understood this item cannot be called done.
close_reason: Done (v0.33.0). The server-side renewal timer at lock_ttl/3 through a Drop-free LeaseRenewer shipped in PR #58 — chosen over option (a) (renew at object-write boundaries: a single PUT can itself exceed the TTL) and option (b) (a library background thread: 'no background threads' is a property of the sync core, and the server is already async). The only thing keeping this open was the idle-writer reproduction, which now passes as part of the normal cluster suite. Docs updated: lock_ttl no longer needs sizing against the largest expected batch.

title: cluster mode follow-ups: CAS-fenced manifest writes, real-bucket verification
description: Phase 5 (nidus-vuq.5) shipped cooperating-instances cluster mode: Config::cluster, a renewing+fencing writer lease (op-driven, no background thread), and the manifest as a universal commit counter so ReadOnly readers refresh() per commit. Hardening follow-ups, none blocking: (1) CAS-fenced manifest/segment writes — the lease is renewed+verified at each batch START (the primary fence), but a writer that pauses > lock_ttl *mid-batch* (e.g. a long GC pause between renew and the manifest PUT) could still be superseded yet clobber. Close this with a conditional/compare-and-swap manifest PUT (S3 If-Match:<etag> / GCS ifGenerationMatch=<gen>) keyed on the expected current version — needs ETag/generation plumbing beyond the existing create-if-absent (nidus-a7c). (2) Real S3/GCS cluster verification — the lease takes the race-free try_create_exclusive path; verify acquire/renew/fence/takeover against real buckets (the in-RAM InMemObjectStore covers the logic). (3) Tier-aware refresh in cluster — adopt the shared memory-tier working-set snapshot on refresh instead of replaying the log (overlaps nidus-bdg). (4) Doc/guard the single idle-writer-past-TTL takeover window (lock_ttl tuning).

SHIPPED (PR: cluster-cas-and-incremental-refresh, v0.23.0): CAS-fenced cluster writes. New Persistence::get_cas/put_cas (opaque token; CasOutcome) implemented for S3 (If-Match/If-None-Match ETag), GCS (ifGenerationMatch), and the in-RAM test store; try_create_exclusive now delegates to put_cas (deduped). Every cluster-writer durable object write (data/log/segments via ObjectAppender, manifest via persist_manifest) is now a compare-and-swap on the version last seen, so a writer superseded mid-batch is REFUSED rather than clobbering committed data — closes the mid-batch split-brain window the per-batch lease could not. Verified in-RAM (cluster_cas_fences_a_superseded_writer_and_preserves_committed_data, cluster_manifest_commit_is_compare_and_swapped) + offline S3 mock round-trip + GCS URI unit tests; all Miri-clean. Tier-aware refresh sub-item delivered under nidus-bdg.

The 'cannot run cloud in dev env' blocker on item 2 dissolves — minio gives real S3 ETag/If-Match semantics with no cloud creds. After 1e6.3 lands, what remains here is genuinely-cloud-only: actual AWS S3 + GCS bucket behaviour (IAM, real consistency, GCS ifGenerationMatch against Google's service) and the lock_ttl tuning docs.

title: refresh follow-ups: incremental delta refresh, tier-aware adopt, change-callback
description: Phase 4 shipped Nidus::refresh() (PR for nidus-vuq.4): a ReadOnly reader re-reads the manifest+log and adopts a writer's newer state in place. It currently does a FULL re-open of the segment set + a FULL log replay on any change. Follow-ups to make it cheaper / richer: (1) Incremental refresh — re-read only the active segment's appended-rows delta and the new log tail since loaded_log_offset, instead of re-opening every segment and replaying from zero (O(delta) not O(N)); seal/compaction can stay on the full path. (2) Tier-aware refresh — when a shared memory tier is configured, try_adopt its working-set snapshot (matching row_count+watermark) on refresh instead of replaying the log, mirroring the open path. (3) Optional change-notification hook so a host can learn a refresh found new state without polling. All additive; none needed until a real cooperating-reader workload asks for it (single-node refresh is already correct and cheap-when-unchanged).
notes: SHIPPED (PR: cluster-cas-and-incremental-refresh, v0.23.0): incremental + tier-aware refresh. refresh() now (1) adopts a shared memory-tier snapshot matching the new row-count+watermark, skipping the log replay (mirrors open); (2) on the no-restructure path (segment LIST unchanged — plain appends, no seal/compaction) re-reads ONLY the active segment object and reuses every immutable segment via Segments::reopen_active/install_active, avoiding the dominant object-store cost of re-fetching the whole set; a seal/compaction (list changed) takes the full re-open. 'restructured' keys on the segment list, not the manifest version (which in cluster mode is the per-commit counter). Atomic: all fallible IO into locals, one infallible swap. Verified: cluster_incremental_refresh_skips_immutable_segments (GET-count asserts the immutable base is not re-fetched) + existing refresh_* parity tests; Miri-clean. REMAINING (keep open, low priority): true O(delta) active-segment read via a range/partial GET (currently re-reads the whole active object) needs a Persistence range-read primitive; optional change-notification hook (refresh already returns adopted? bool, so not needed until a real workload asks).

title: mmap follow-ups: runtime seal-to-mmap, ReadOnly active-segment map, object-store cold cache, madvise, big-endian
description: Phase 3 (nidus-vuq.3) shipped per-segment mmap as an open-time decision over local-FS immutable segments. Deferred, additive follow-ups over the same seam: (1) runtime seal-to-mmap — a long-running writer keeps just-sealed segments in RAM until reopen; dropping the RAM copy and mapping on seal would give >RAM within one process lifetime. (2) mmap the active/last segment in ReadOnly opens — a search-only reader of a single large segment can't currently map it (only non-active segments are mapped). (3) object-store cold cache — download remote (s3/gs) segments to a local cache file then mmap; mmap is local-FS-only today. (4) madvise(SEQUENTIAL/RANDOM/WILLNEED) hints to tune paging for the scan pattern. (5) big-endian hosts fall back to RAM load (the zero-copy cast is little-endian only) — add a converting mmap path if a BE target ever matters. None are needed at nidus's local-first scale; file-and-defer.

description:
Follow-ups deferred from Phase 2 (nidus-vuq.2), all additive over the shipped segment+IVF format:
1. Persist per-segment IVF indexes as their own cache objects (e.g. seg-NNNNNNNN.ivf) so open() loads instead of rebuilding from scratch. Today every per-segment IVF is rebuilt on open (immutable segments, cheap k-means) — fine for now, but a cache avoids O(indexed rows) k-means on every open of a large store. Mirror the existing ann/fts cache codec + validity-key pattern (dedupe).
2. Parallel + quantized per-segment walks: build/search the per-segment IVFs under query_threads and let them score quant codes (the global ann path already does both via Walk). Today per-segment uses Walk::exact, serial-ish build.
3. Expose per-segment IVF tuning (n_lists/n_probe/overscan/seed) instead of the fixed AnnConfig::ivf() defaults.
4. Background segment-merge / compaction of many small sealed segments into fewer larger indexed ones (SPEC §14.2 'background merge').

title: Phase 5: cluster mode (shared backend + writer lease + fencing)
description: Cluster mode as a CONSEQUENCE of the segment model: segments+WAL+manifest on a SHARED persistence backend are the shared truth; instances are stateless caches. One writer appends segments + advances the manifest, elected by the §6.3 writer lock (race-free over object stores, nidus-a7c) evolved into a heartbeated LEASE; fence segment/manifest writes so a superseded-but-alive writer can't clobber (reuse the a7c conditional-PUT plumbing). Readers refresh per phase 4. Requires shared persistence AND shared memory tier; reject local FS/local RAM for cluster mode with a clear error. SPEC §14.6 phase 5.
close_reason: Shipped (0.22.0): cooperating-instances cluster mode via Config::cluster — the SPEC §14.6 phase-5 shared-backend model (1 writer + N readers), lightweight (no coordinator/replication/rebalancing). (1) Writer LEASE (src/backend/object.rs ClusterLease): the object writer-lock evolved to carry an owner token, acquired race-free via try_create_exclusive, RENEWED op-driven on every write batch in check_writable() (no background thread, honouring the sync/no-threads design), and FENCING — a superseded writer (taken over while paused past lock_ttl) fails its next write instead of clobbering. (2) Manifest = universal COMMIT COUNTER: every durable batch bumps+republishes the manifest version (Segments::bump_version + note_cluster_commit in maybe_sync/upsert/flush), so a ReadOnly reader detects any commit (not just seals) with one manifest read via refresh() (phase 4) — works on object stores where log length isn't live cross-process. (3) Config gating: cluster requires shared object-store persistence AND a shared memory tier; local FS / process RAM rejected with a clear error. No new deps; §4 public API unchanged (cluster is config-only). Tests: 7 store-level (object_backed, Miri-clean) + 3 lease unit (backend, Miri-clean) + 1 file-backed local-FS rejection. Follow-ups (CAS-fenced manifest writes for the mid-batch-pause window, real-bucket verification, tier-aware refresh): nidus-ahw. Epic nidus-vuq now fully complete (5/5).

title: Phase 4: manifest-versioned reader refresh
description: Version the manifest; a reader detects a newer manifest and adopts it atomically (swap the pointer, then drop segments no longer referenced) — a consistent snapshot, never a torn mix. Foundation for cooperating instances seeing fresh writes without a full reopen. SPEC §14.6 phase 4 + consistency note.
close_reason: Shipped (0.21.0): Nidus::refresh() -> Result<bool> advances a lock-free ReadOnly reader to a writer's newer committed state in place — re-reads the manifest, and when the version advanced (seal/compaction) or the log grew (append/delete) re-opens the segment set + replays the log into a fresh index at one consistent point, swapped in atomically (segment-open/log-read run before any self mutation, so a concurrent-compaction race leaves the prior snapshot serving). Cheap no-op when current (manifest read + log stat). Composes with mmap, per-segment IVF, quantization. Change detection: manifest.version (Segments::version()) + loaded_log_offset watermark. New public API additive (SPEC §14.5 honoured). Follow-ups in nidus-bdg.

title: Phase 2: Shared memory tier (Redis/Valkey/Memcached) — model (a), loaded into local RAM
description: First network backend and the proof the trait holds for a LIVE store. Use redis-rs in blocking mode (pure Rust, sync). redis:// needs no TLS. Maps the append capability natively (APPEND / streams), so it exercises the live write path without the object-store whole-object-rewrite problem. Gated behind a non-default feature so the pure library is untouched. Document the open-cost / shared-state-across-processes tradeoffs (SPEC §13.4/§13.5).
acceptance_criteria: redis:// store opens, upserts, searches, and reopens against a real Redis/Valkey; append maps to a native incremental op; feature-gated; version bumped.
notes: RECATEGORIZED: NOT a durable storage backend with native append. It is the MEMORY TIER (SPEC §13.3) — a shared, rebuildable cache of the serialized in-RAM working set (vectors + derived indexes), pulled into local RAM to serve. Wins: N stateless workers share one copy; restart = load not rebuild. Pure-Rust sync (redis-rs blocking, plain TCP redis://, no TLS). Memcached = evictable cache-only, weakest. Rebuildable from persistence, so empty/evicted is never fatal.

title: Cache the row-sorted scan order across queries
description: search() now collects in-scope rows into a Vec and sort_unstable_by_key(row) on EVERY query to get sequential data-matrix access (the big win in nidus-33k). The doc set only changes on upsert/delete, so this sorted order is recomputed redundantly across the many queries between writes. Optimization: maintain a row-sorted index (or lazily cache + invalidate on write) so steady-state search skips the per-query O(n) alloc + O(n log n) sort. Must stay correct under multi-collection scope, filters, dead rows (append-only overwrite), and Miri-clean. Measure with just bench-crit against the nidus-33k-final baseline; only worth it if it beats the already-strong current numbers without complicating the write path. Filed from nidus-33k.
notes:
Measured 2026-06-05 while doing nidus-8gx (which changed the sort landscape).

FINDINGS:
- sort_unstable_by_key on the scan is ~2.16 ms standalone at n=100k, dim=768
  (micro-bench: clone+sort and sort-only both ~2.15 ms). That's ~29% of the
  7.45 ms serial f32 query, and it scales with n. So caching it is a real win
  for LARGE-n SINGLE-query SERIAL search.
- The sort itself is ESSENTIAL and stays: skipping it (random HashMap-order
  access) blows the serial query from 7.45 ms to 22 ms (~3x slower) because
  sequential data-matrix access is the cache-friendliness win from nidus-33k.
  dxt must KEEP sorted access and only remove the per-query RECOMPUTE.

POST-8gx SCOPE NARROWED:
- 8gx made the parallel path sort PER-CHUNK inside workers (global sort skipped
  there). So dxt now only helps the SERIAL path directly. A cached global order
  could let the parallel path skip per-chunk sorts too (composes well), but the
  at-scale recommendation is now query_threads / quant, not serial.

WRITE-PATH / SYNC TENSION (the issue's gating concern):
- Store is used as Arc<RwLock<Nidus>>, so the cache cannot use RefCell (not
  Sync). Clean options: (a) lazy global cache behind RwLock<Option<Vec>> +
  dirty flag (write path just flips the flag; ~2% extra RAM for duplicated
  id/col strings; one rebuild after each write batch); (b) per-collection
  append-order index exploiting monotonic rows (no RwLock, but overwrites/
  deletes need validation-or-fallback + multi-collection needs k-way merge);
  (c) row-major doc table refactor (eliminates the sort for ALL paths, cleanest
  end state, but large higher-risk refactor across every read/write path).

DECISION 2026-06-05: deferred by user. Benefit is real but narrow post-8gx and
every clean capture touches RAM or the write path. Revisit if a consumer hits
large-n serial search as the hot path. If picked up, (a) is the recommended
low-risk start; (c) is the right long-term shape on its own branch.
2026-06-09: Pulled into nidus-3zg (binary quant + shared scan-order cache). The scan-order cache is specced as a component there — implement together so all scan paths (serial/parallel f32, int8, binary) share one row-sorted index. Tracking the cache work under 3zg; keeping dxt open as the linked detail/rationale.
close_reason: Shipped via nidus-3zg as recommended option (a): lazy global cache behind RwLock<Option<ScanOrder>> (src/store/mod.rs:164) built in Store::scan_order (src/store/read.rs:196) and invalidated on write (src/store/write.rs:153,426,476,675). Steady-state search no longer recomputes the O(n log n) sort per query.
